steps: Confirm the phenotype and target

Decide whether this is adductor spasmodic dysphonia, abductor spasmodic dysphonia or essential vocal tremor, because that sets the muscle: thyroarytenoid for adductor and most tremor, posterior cricoarytenoid for abductor. Review prior dose, side, duration of benefit and any breathiness or thin-liquid dysphagia. Ask about bleeding disorders and anticoagulants, and note prior laryngeal surgery or infection that may distort the percutaneous route.
Choose the starting dose

For adductor disease a common start is 2.5 units in 0.1 mL into each thyroarytenoid; halve it for elderly or small-framed patients. A unilateral regimen uses a larger one-side dose, and cricothyroid or strap muscles are options when EMG or the clinical pattern points there. For abductor disease, give 3.75 to 10 units split between two sites in one posterior cricoarytenoid.
Position and connect the EMG

Seat the patient semi-reclined with the neck partly, not fully, extended so the cricothyroid space opens without stretching the skin taut. Place the reference electrode on the forehead and the ground lead, and run the monitor before skin entry to clear 60-cycle interference. Sedation is not needed; keep oxygen and suction available.
Palpate and mark landmarks

Feel the hyoid, thyroid notch, lower border of the thyroid cartilage, cricoid arch and the cricothyroid membrane between them, then mark the midline. Landmarks are harder to find in obese or irradiated necks; take time here, because a wrong starting point is the usual reason the needle ends up in strap muscle or the airway.
Anesthetize sparingly

Raise a small superficial weal of 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine over the midline cricothyroid membrane (and about 1 cm below the cricoid if the cricothyroid muscle is a target). Use only a fraction of a milliliter: too much local swells the tissue and hides the cartilage edges you need to steer by. Topical laryngeal anesthesia is not required.
Fix the skin over the membrane

With the nondominant index and middle fingers in the cricothyroid space, press gently to pin the skin and shorten the distance from skin to membrane. This keeps the entry point from sliding as the needle passes and gives a steadier feel for the membrane as it gives way.
Pass the needle to the thyroarytenoid

Use a Teflon-coated hollow monopolar EMG injection needle. Enter at or just off the midline, pierce the cricothyroid membrane and angle superolaterally toward the vocal fold, usually 1.5 to 4 cm from skin depending on neck thickness. Stay submucosal under the fold; the aim is muscle, not the laryngeal lumen.
Read the EMG to correct position

Too superficial gives sternohyoid (fires with head lift) or cricothyroid (rises with high pitch). Too deep passes through the fold toward the posterior cricoarytenoid. Too medial enters the airway: the tracing goes to a hollow air artifact and the patient coughs. Withdraw slightly and redirect rather than injecting on a doubtful signal.
Confirm activation before injecting

Ask for a sustained /i/, a glottal stop or a breath hold; the thyroarytenoid shows brisk, dense recruitment at once, while the lateral cricoarytenoid gives a burst at phonation onset. Do not inject on surface anatomy alone. If a flexible scope is in place, small needle movements can be matched to fold motion.
Inject a small volume and repeat as planned

Deliver the dose in about 0.1 mL, withdraw, and repeat on the other side only if the plan is bilateral and symmetric. Minimize passes through the airway, which provoke cough and spread toxin onto mucosa. Expect coughing or a swallow during confirmation; pause and resettle rather than pushing through it.
Abductor disease: inject one posterior cricoarytenoid at a time

Reach the posterior cricoarytenoid percutaneously (rotating the larynx to approach behind the thyroid lamina) or transorally under videostroboscopic guidance. Confirm with a sniff, which activates this abductor. Inject two sites in one muscle, then treat the opposite side at a separate visit, usually 2 to 4 weeks later, to avoid bilateral abductor weakness and airway compromise.
Know the other targets

When supraglottic squeeze dominates, the false vocal fold can be injected percutaneously in clinic. After total laryngectomy, constrictor hypertonicity that blocks tracheoesophageal speech responds to toxin divided among cricopharyngeus and inferior and middle constrictors, but only after transnasal esophagoscopy has excluded stricture and recurrence and the prosthesis is confirmed patent.
Observe and counsel

Watch for about 30 minutes for bleeding, vasovagal symptoms or airway reaction; endoscope the larynx if injury is a concern. Warn the patient that breathiness and choking on thin liquids may appear over the first one to two weeks before the voice improves, and advise small sips and a chin tuck until it settles.
Document and titrate

Record muscle, side, dose, dilution and EMG findings. If there is no effect by about 2 weeks, re-inject; doses given less than 6 to 8 weeks apart count as boosters and add to the prior dose. With a good response, repeat at roughly 3 to 4 months, and raise the dose only if benefit is long and side effects are absent.

Percutaneous PCA access detail (larynx rotation) and the dysphagia counseling are standard practice, not from Iowa. No disagreement with the current card.

steps: Assemble and test before induction

Choose bronchoscope diameter and length for age, and have one size smaller open. Build the telescope, light and camera, and pick the optical forceps for the expected object before starting; changing mid-case wastes apnea time. Preload the matched suction catheter, which is awkward to place once in the airway, and keep a flexible bronchoscope available.
Agree the ventilation plan

Discuss with anesthesia how the patient will breathe: spontaneous ventilation is preferred for most foreign bodies, with controlled ventilation through the side port once the scope is in. In children, mask induction is typical and the bed is turned 90 degrees toward the surgeon. If a laser is planned, agree on the lowest workable FiO2.
Expose the larynx and topicalize

Lift with a Macintosh or Miller blade to view the glottis, spray the vocal folds with lidocaine within the weight-based maximum dose, then re-expose to confirm the view. Topical anesthesia reduces laryngospasm and coughing when the scope passes. Protect the teeth or gums from the blade throughout.
Pass the glottis with the bevel turned

Advance the bronchoscope under telescope vision. As the tip nears the larynx, rotate it 90 degrees so the leading edge lies parallel to the vocal folds and slips between them rather than catching a fold; then rotate back. Remove the laryngoscope once the scope is through, and keep the lips clear of the barrel.
Connect ventilation and suction

Attach the anesthesia circuit to the side port, confirm chest rise and end-tidal carbon dioxide, and advance the preloaded suction. Cover the eyepiece port when ventilating through the scope so pressure is not lost. Short, planned apneic periods during instrument changes should be coordinated with the anesthetist.
Advance through subglottis and trachea

Move forward under continuous vision, keeping the posterior membranous wall as the orientation landmark. Note the subglottic lumen, tracheal rings and the normal motion of the posterior wall with breathing, and look for stenosis, malacia, external compression or secretions before reaching the carina.
Enter each mainstem by turning the head

Turn the head to the right to align the scope with the left mainstem bronchus, and to the left to enter the right. Inspect the carina and both mainstems systematically, then the lobar orifices as scope size allows, including the right upper lobe origin just below the carina, which is easy to pass by.
Document before you intervene

Record stenosis, lesion, secretion burden, dynamic collapse or foreign body, with photographs, before manipulating anything. Once bleeding or edema starts, the baseline view is lost. For a foreign body, note its type, orientation and whether granulation tissue surrounds it, since that changes the grasp.
Biopsy or debride with control

Keep forceps and energy devices in the visual field at all times. Coordinate low FiO2 and laser-fire precautions. Topical dilute epinephrine helps hemostasis, but warn anesthesia if the patient takes beta-blockers, as unopposed alpha effect can cause a hypertensive crisis.
Set up the foreign body grasp

Hold the bronchoscope steady just proximal to the object, remove the telescope and bridge, and pass the optical forceps loaded with the camera. Approach the object so the jaws can close on its most stable part; for round objects, a cup or basket forceps or a balloon passed beyond it is safer than repeated slipping grasps.
Withdraw scope and object as a unit

Once grasped, pull the forceps back against the bronchoscope tip and withdraw forceps, object and scope together, rather than drawing the object through the scope or pushing it distally. Slow down at the glottis, where a large object is most likely to be stripped off; if dropped there, re-secure the airway first.
Reinspect the whole airway

Reinsert the bronchoscope and look again in both mainstems for residual fragments, a second object, bleeding or mucosal injury, and confirm bilateral ventilation. Suction the trachea on withdrawal. Organic material often fragments, so a clear first pass does not guarantee a clear airway.
Look at the upper esophagus

After airway work, examine the upper esophagus for foreign material. Esophageal objects can cause airway symptoms, and children sometimes ingest and aspirate at the same time. Remove the bronchoscope under vision.
Plan observation for edema and pulmonary edema

Decide the level of postoperative monitoring by the intervention, edema, bleeding and oxygen need. Watch for postobstructive pulmonary edema: it usually appears soon after relief of an acute obstruction such as a foreign body, but can be delayed up to 24 hours, and presents with hypoxia and frothy secretions.

steps: Treat it as an immediate emergency

An esophageal button battery causes injury by current, alkaline liquefaction and pressure, and perforation has been reported within about 5 hours. Confirm location on radiographs (a double-ring or halo outline on the frontal view separates it from a coin), then go straight to the operating room without delaying for nonessential tests.
Secure the airway

Intubate before instrumenting; a proximal battery can compress the airway, and extraction may be prolonged or bloody. Have rigid and flexible esophagoscopes, suspension laryngoscopes and a range of graspers ready, since injury can make the stone-like battery hard to free from swollen mucosa.
Expose a proximal battery directly

Batteries of 1.5 to 2 cm commonly lodge at the cricopharyngeus. At this level, a suspension laryngoscope placed into the hypopharynx, with a laryngeal lift to open the introitus, can expose the battery for removal under direct vision. Lower batteries need rigid or flexible esophagoscopy.
Assess and note the negative pole

Before grasping, look at the surrounding mucosa and note which face of the battery points to which wall. The negative pole (the narrower side, opposite the side marked +) produces the most severe injury, so knowing its orientation tells you where to look hardest afterward and which structure, airway or aorta, is at risk.
Remove along the esophageal axis

Grasp a stable edge and withdraw the battery in line with the esophagus without fragmenting it, prolonged manipulation or pushing it distally. If it is embedded, gently free the rim rather than levering it against necrotic wall. A protective overtube or withdrawal into a rigid scope helps protect the injured wall.
Reinspect the injury circumferentially

Reinsert the scope and assess depth of necrosis, any perforation, bleeding and the level relative to the trachea and aortic arch. Expect the worst injury on the wall that faced the negative pole. Measure the length of injury, which often extends several centimeters below the battery site.
Leave adherent necrosis alone

Avoid aggressive debridement of adherent slough: it may be sealing a contained perforation or a weakened vessel wall. Gentle irrigation is acceptable, but do not scrape the bed. If perforation is seen, stop instrumenting and move to imaging and surgical planning.
Survey for other objects

Check the rest of the esophagus and stomach for additional batteries or material, especially when the history is uncertain, and document the exact level and severity of mucosal injury with photographs for comparison at the second look.
Plan a second-look esophagoscopy

Injury keeps progressing after removal, so re-examine at about 24 to 48 hours to see the full extent of damage. Abort the procedure if a perforation is found. Use the second look, together with imaging, to decide feeding route and how long to restrict oral intake.
Set NPO, imaging and feeding plan

Institute NPO status and arrange contrast imaging and feeding access according to injury depth. When the battery sat near the aorta, plan contrast CT or MRI to assess vascular risk. Give antibiotics only when perforation or mediastinitis is present or suspected.
Monitor for delayed catastrophe

Keep explicit precautions for aorto-esophageal hemorrhage and tracheoesophageal fistula, which can occur days to weeks after removal; tracheoesophageal fistula is well described. Herald bleeding, new cough with feeding or chest pain requires immediate evaluation, and families must know these warning signs.
Follow for stricture

Deep circumferential injuries often heal with stricture. Arrange follow-up esophagram or endoscopy once healing is under way, and counsel families on dysphagia symptoms. Use the event to teach battery safety, since most ingestions involve batteries removed from devices.

steps: Confirm the diagnosis and timing

Review imaging and examination to define the arch and course. In adults, treat a lateral neck cyst as possible cystic metastasis (oropharyngeal or thyroid) until proven otherwise. Operate when the lesion is quiet: treat active infection first, since a recently infected tract is scarred and harder to follow.
Anesthesia and draping

Use general endotracheal anesthesia without long-acting paralysis so the facial, hypoglossal and other nerves can be stimulated. Drape so the face is visible to watch for facial twitch, and for a first-cleft lesion include the auricle and ear canal in the field. Have a nerve stimulator, lacrimal probes and methylene blue ready.
Mark the tract

For a sinus or fistula, cannulate the external opening with a fine lacrimal probe or inject dilute methylene blue to mark the tract before incising. For a first-cleft lesion, examine the ear canal under the microscope for a canal opening or web. Mark incisions in relaxed skin lines and infiltrate with dilute epinephrine.
First cleft: parotidectomy-style access

For anomalies near the angle of the mandible, ear canal or parotid, plan a parotidectomy-type incision, incorporating any pit or involved skin in an ellipse. Raise the skin flap over the parotid fascia. Do not cut through the tract as you dissect near the tragal cartilage, which is close to where the tract often runs.
First cleft: find the facial nerve first

Identify the main facial nerve trunk as in a superficial parotidectomy before following the tract, because it may run superficial to, deep to or between the branches. Keep the nerve in view throughout and use the stimulator to confirm branches rather than relying on appearance.
First cleft: excise to the canal

Under direct view of the nerve, remove the cyst and tract with a thin cuff of parotid tissue, following it to the canal. Excise any involved canal skin or a small piece of cartilage where the tract ends. Stimulate the nerve afterward and pack the canal to support the canal skin.
Second to fourth cleft: incisions

Make a horizontal skin-crease incision at or just above a cyst, or a small ellipse around a sinus opening. For a long tract, add one or two higher stepladder incisions rather than one long vertical scar; the tract can be passed up beneath the skin bridge to the next incision.
Raise flaps and define the lesion

Elevate subplatysmal flaps, protecting the marginal mandibular nerve superiorly. Develop the cyst or tract circumferentially with its capsule intact and define its relation to the sternocleidomastoid, carotid sheath and cranial nerves before following it deeply.
Second cleft: follow the course

Follow the tract superiorly between the internal and external carotid arteries, superficial to the glossopharyngeal and hypoglossal nerves and deep to the posterior digastric and stylohyoid, toward the tonsillar fossa. Identify and protect the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves at this stage.
Third and fourth pouch lesions

A third-cleft tract runs behind the internal carotid, between the glossopharyngeal nerve above and hypoglossal nerve below, and enters the pyriform sinus just above the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Find the pyriform opening by direct laryngoscopy; endoscopic cauterization is accepted, while open excision may need hemithyroidectomy with recurrent and superior laryngeal nerve protection.
Dissect under vision, not traction

Control feeding vessels and divide scarred attachments sharply under direct visualization rather than avulsing with traction, which tears the tract and leaves epithelium behind. Blunt and sharp dissection along the tract wall keeps you out of the carotid and off the nerves.
Ligate the pharyngeal end

Follow the epithelial tract to its endpoint. When it reaches the pharynx, suture-ligate it at the pharyngeal wall and divide it, removing the cyst and full tract to minimize recurrence. Leaving a segment of tract is the main cause of recurrence.
Check nerves and hemostasis

Inspect the carotid sheath and the nerves encountered and confirm function with the stimulator: facial nerve for first-cleft lesions, hypoglossal, glossopharyngeal and superior laryngeal for lower lesions. Irrigate and obtain meticulous hemostasis.
Close and follow up

Close in layers and place a drain when dead space warrants it (some surgeons drain routinely, removing it at one to two days as output falls). Remove skin sutures at about five to seven days, and confirm benign pathology, particularly in adults.

steps: Confirm candidacy and choose the side

Recheck criteria and drug-induced sleep endoscopy: no complete concentric palatal collapse, and few central or mixed events. Choose the implant side in advance (commonly right, though some centers default to left), keeping the generator at least 15 cm from any other implanted device and away from the shoulder a patient braces a firearm against.
Anesthesia without lasting paralysis

Intubate orally and tape the tube to the side opposite the implant. Use only short-acting relaxants so the nerve can be mapped. Keep the ipsilateral arm free of IV, blood pressure cuff and oximeter, and the ipsilateral chest free of ECG leads. Turn the head away from the implant side; a shoulder roll is optional.
Place tongue electrodes, prep and drape

Before prepping, insert NIM electrodes: one into the hyoglossus in the ventrolateral tongue (retractor) and one into the genioglossus lateral to the frenulum, in front of the duct (protrusor). Prep from lower lip to xiphoid. Isolate the mouth with a clear adhesive drape so tongue movement stays visible. Avoid monopolar cautery near the nerve and leads.
Make the neck incision

Make a horizontal upper-neck incision below the mandible, about midway between mandible and hyoid and just off the midline. Divide platysma and raise a small subplatysmal flap, protecting the marginal mandibular nerve, which lies superficial in this field.
Expose the hypoglossal nerve

Mobilize the anteroinferior submandibular gland and retract it posterosuperiorly. Retract the digastric tendon inferiorly with a vessel loop. Find the posterior border of the mylohyoid and retract it anteriorly to reveal the nerve beneath; control or divide the ranine veins. The lingual nerve lies superior and deep, so stay on the hypoglossal.
Map the branches

Loop the nerve and bring in the microscope. Stimulate to find the functional breakpoint, dissect focally there and remap. Include the medial branches to the genioglossus (protrusors), the transverse and vertical intrinsic muscles and the C1 branch to the geniohyoid; exclude the lateral branches to the hyoglossus and styloglossus (retrusors). The vasa nervorum often marks the division.
Place and anchor the cuff

Place the stimulation cuff around the selected distal branches without stretching or compressing the nerve. Anchor the lead with silk sutures and a strain-relief loop. Stimulate through the cuff and confirm forward tongue protrusion without retraction or depression; if retraction occurs, a retrusor branch is captured and the cuff must be repositioned.
Create the generator pocket

Make a chest incision about 3 cm below the clavicle (or over the second to third rib space, about 3 cm lateral to the sternal edge). Dissect to the pectoralis fascia and create a pocket about three fingerbreadths wide, sized so the generator lies flat without tension on the skin.
Inspire IV only: place the sensing lead

Through the pectoralis, divide the fat pad beneath it and identify external intercostal fibers, which run superolateral to inferomedial. Incise the thin muscle near its medial edge and slide a narrow bent malleable retractor, without resistance and parallel to the rib, into the plane between the external and internal intercostals. Place the lead there, anchored with silk, avoiding pleural entry. Inspire V has no separate sensing lead.
Check for pneumothorax

If a sensing lead was placed, fill the wound with saline and ask anesthesia for a positive-pressure breath; bubbling suggests a pleural leak. Obtain a chest radiograph if pneumothorax is suspected, and repair any pleural opening before closing.
Tunnel the stimulation lead

Pass the tunneler from the neck to the chest pocket deep to the platysma but over the clavicle, then pull the stimulation lead through. Leave enough slack at both ends so neck movement does not tether or dislodge the cuff, and avoid sharp kinks.
Connect and seat the generator

Connect stimulation and sensing leads to the generator and seat it in the pocket, securing it to the fascia. Coil excess lead beneath the generator and keep the leads lying flat, since a raised loop under thin skin is a common site of extrusion.
Test the whole system

With the telemetry wand in a sterile sleeve, stimulate through the device and confirm tongue protrusion without retraction. With Inspire IV, confirm a clean respiratory waveform from the sensing lead. Revise cuff position if activation is retrusive, before closing.
Close without compressing hardware

Obtain hemostasis, irrigate both wounds and close in layers with buried absorbable sutures and skin glue. Avoid tight dressings that compress the generator or leads. Obtain a chest film to document generator and leads, and a lateral neck film to document the cuff position.
Recovery and activation

Most patients go home the same day or after overnight observation and resume diet once awake. Check tongue movement and wounds at one to two days, limit strenuous activity for about 4 weeks, and activate the device at about 1 month, with sleep study titration a few months later.

step: Identify the gland correctly

Distinguish parathyroid from fat, thyroid nodule and node: parathyroid is tan to light brown against yellow fat, with a discrete capsule, its own pedicle and a soft, mobile feel when nudged with a Kittner. A thin fascial layer often covers it; opening that layer lets it roll free. Check thyroid clefts, so a gland is not hidden under the retractor. Use any normal ipsilateral gland as this patient's reference.
Autotransplant a devascularized normal gland

If a normal gland darkens or loses its pedicle, set it aside in cold saline, confirm parathyroid on frozen section of a small fragment, and mince it into about 1 mm pieces. Place them in one or more sternocleidomastoid pockets and mark the site with a nonabsorbable suture and a clip, so the graft can be found if hyperparathyroidism recurs.
Intraoperative PTH after excision

Draw PTH at set times after removal, commonly 5 and 10 minutes. The Miami criterion is a fall of more than 50% from the highest pre-incision or pre-excision value by 10 minutes; some also require a normal value. Handling the gland can spike PTH, so a 15 to 20 minute draw helps when early values are ambiguous. A slow or partial fall means keep the operation open.
Inadequate PTH fall: convert

Lengthen the incision and look at the second gland on the same side, then explore the other side; also convert when only three normal glands are found. Palpate the tracheoesophageal groove and esophagus into the posterior mediastinum, check retroesophageal and retropharyngeal spaces, carotid sheath, behind the tubercle of Zuckerkandl and inside the thyroid. Deliver the thymus with gentle traction. For four-gland hyperplasia, remove three and a half glands.

steps: Assemble equipment before induction

Have age-appropriate rigid ventilating bronchoscopes, telescopes, and rescue sizes open on the field. Preload the color-matched flexible suction catheter into the bronchoscope, because it is difficult to place once the scope is in the airway. Keep a small flexible bronchoscope available for distal or segmental objects and for a final survey.
Match forceps to the object

Open an optical forceps set sized to the child and the object (infant or child sizes, with very small forceps rarely needed), and load the telescope and light into the chosen forceps in advance. Have nonoptical long forceps, cup or basket instruments, and a magnet-tipped option available for objects that optical forceps cannot hold.
Plan a shared airway

Agree with anesthesia on a plan that keeps the child oxygenated: typically inhalational mask induction maintaining spontaneous ventilation, so a ball-valving or mobile object is not driven distally by positive pressure. Discuss how ventilation will run through the bronchoscope side port and what to do if saturation falls during extraction.
Position and expose the larynx

Turn the table about 90 degrees toward the surgeon once the child is deeply anesthetized. Place a shoulder roll if needed and protect the teeth or gums. Expose the glottis with a Macintosh or Miller laryngoscope blade, suctioning secretions so the vocal folds and any supraglottic or subglottic object are seen first.
Topicalize the vocal folds

Spray the vocal folds and subglottis with 1% lidocaine to blunt laryngospasm and coughing during instrumentation. Calculate the dose by weight before spraying and stay within the maximum (the protocol cites 4 mg/kg), remembering that small children reach toxic doses quickly with repeated applications.
Pass the bronchoscope atraumatically

Re-expose the glottis and advance the rigid bronchoscope with its 0-degree telescope under direct vision. Rotate the scope about 90 degrees as it reaches the larynx so the beveled tip is parallel to the vocal folds and slides between them rather than catching a fold. Then remove the laryngoscope and rotate the bronchoscope back to neutral.
Connect ventilation and survey

Attach the anesthesia circuit to the bronchoscope side port and advance the suction catheter. Survey the trachea and both main bronchi before touching the object, so its position, orientation, surrounding edema or granulation, and the distal airway are understood. Turn the head away from the side being examined to align the scope with each main bronchus.
Stabilize the scope and change instruments

Once the object is seen, hold the bronchoscope still at a fixed depth and remove the telescope and its bridge. Introduce the preloaded optical forceps down the barrel so the object stays in view. Keep the bronchoscope tip just proximal to the object to avoid pushing it deeper.
Grasp under direct vision

Choose a grasp suited to the object: open jaws around its widest part, or use cup or basket instruments for friable organic material such as nuts that fragment. Close firmly under vision and never grasp blindly or advance while grasping. If fragments break off, plan to retrieve each piece rather than pushing pieces distally.
Withdraw as one unit

If the object is larger than the bronchoscope lumen, withdraw the forceps, object, and bronchoscope together as a single unit, keeping the object close to the scope tip. Slow down at the glottis, where objects are most often stripped off. If an object is lost in the subglottis and ventilation fails, push it back into a main bronchus to restore ventilation, then retrieve again.
Re-examine the airway

Reinsert the bronchoscope and inspect the entire trachea and both bronchial trees again for a second object or residual fragments, mucosal tears, granulation, bleeding, and retained secretions. Rotate the head to the right to see the left main bronchus and to the left to see the right. Use the flexible bronchoscope for distal segments.
Clear secretions and treat edema

Suction obstructing secretions and pus from distal segments through the bronchoscope, using a large suction catheter as the scope is withdrawn. Treat bronchospasm and airway edema as needed, for example with bronchodilators and a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone after prolonged or traumatic extraction.
Check the esophagus

Before ending the anesthetic, examine the upper esophagus for a second object, since children who aspirate may also swallow material and some airway symptoms come from an esophageal object compressing the trachea. Then confirm symmetric air entry and adequate oxygenation as the child returns to spontaneous ventilation.
Recover and observe

Monitor for hypoxia, stridor, and postobstructive pulmonary edema, which can follow relief of a high-grade obstruction and may need positive pressure support. Set the observation level by the difficulty of extraction, duration of instrumentation, residual pneumonia or atelectasis, and airway edema. Obtain a chest radiograph when symptoms persist or residual material is suspected.
airway-fb.notes: Replaced the 8-step outline with a 14-step sequence built from the Iowa airway foreign-body protocol: preloaded suction catheter, optical-forceps tray selection, mask induction with the table turned 90 degrees, weight-based lidocaine topicalization (protocol cites 4 mg/kg), the 90-degree bronchoscope rotation through the glottis, telescope-to-forceps exchange while holding the scope still, head turning to view each main bronchus, and esophageal check. All prior card points kept (shared airway, rescue scopes, survey first, matched forceps, withdraw as a unit, second-look, suction, edema/bronchospasm, observation). Pushing a lost object back into a main bronchus and postobstructive pulmonary edema monitoring are standard practice; the edema point comes from the protocol's postoperative section. The Iowa page states it was last updated before 2013.

steps: Plan an awake case

Perform the procedure under local anesthesia with light intravenous sedation so the patient can phonate on request; voice and glottic closure are the intraoperative endpoints. Confirm side and persistence of paralysis on preoperative laryngoscopy. Have arytenoid adduction instruments available in case a posterior glottic gap persists after medialization.
Set up the transnasal scope

Decongest and topically anesthetize one nostril, then pass a flexible laryngoscope to confirm the paralyzed side and baseline gap. Turn the table away from anesthesia, give supplemental oxygen, and drape so the face above the lips stays outside the sterile field, keeping the scope usable throughout the case.
Infiltrate with restraint

Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine along the incision, over the thyroid prominence, the ipsilateral thyroid lamina, and its lower border. Avoid large volumes or deep injection near the paraglottic space, because the fluid itself medializes the fold and makes intraoperative voice and scope assessment misleading.
Incise and divide the straps

Make a horizontal skin incision in a neck crease over the middle of the thyroid cartilage, extended toward the paralyzed side. Raise subplatysmal flaps, separate the strap muscles in the midline, and retract them laterally on the operative side to expose the thyroid lamina.
Expose the thyroid lamina

Incise the outer perichondrium in the midline and elevate it laterally off the ipsilateral lamina, exposing the inferior border down to the cricothyroid membrane and back toward the posterior edge. Release cricothyroid muscle slips at the inferior tubercle if needed. A hook or heavy suture in the thyroid prominence rotates the larynx toward the opposite side.
Mark the window

For an expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) implant, outline a window about 5 by 10 mm. Place its lower edge about 3 mm above the inferior border so a solid inferior strut remains, its anterior edge 7 to 10 mm behind the midline, and its upper edge at vocal-fold level, roughly midway between the thyroid notch and the lower border.
Cut the window

Cut the outline with a blade in soft cartilage, or with a small fluted drill when the lamina is ossified, using light pressure so the bit does not plunge into the soft tissue beneath. Keep the inferior strut intact; fracturing it removes the support the implant is wedged against. Control bleeding with bipolar cautery.
Develop the paraglottic pocket

Elevate the inner perichondrium through the window with fine elevators, releasing it posteriorly, inferiorly, and superiorly as needed but not anteriorly, and never enter the laryngeal mucosa. Separate the cricothyroid membrane from the lower border of the cartilage to create a second, inferior access route into the paraglottic space beneath the strut.
Find the target position

Push the paraglottic tissues medially with a blunt elevator from the inferior route while the patient phonates and the fold is watched on the scope. Note the depth and position, usually at the level of the membranous fold, that gives the strongest voice and best closure without airway narrowing or excessive posterior pressure.
Insert the implant

Cut a continuous strip about 1 cm wide from a 0.6 mm Gore-Tex sheet. Feed it from the inferior route under the strut and out through the window, then layer it into the paraglottic space with the elevator, folding it evenly against the inner perichondrium and avoiding lumps (knuckling) that create uneven contour.
Adjust and overcorrect

Add or reposition implant in small increments while the patient phonates and the scope shows fold position. Target the membranous fold, keep the airway adequate, and check height so the fold is not pushed above or below the opposite side. Once the best voice is reached, medialize about 2 mm more to allow for resolving edema; the voice should sound slightly pressed.
Secure the implant

Trim the excess strip. Pass a fine nonabsorbable monofilament (polypropylene) suture under the inferior strut and through the implant, then run it over the window in a hammock and anchor it through cartilage above the window, or a small drill hole if ossified. This prevents extrusion into the neck or migration.
Add arytenoid adduction if needed

If the scope still shows a posterior glottic gap or the vocal process sits at a different height, add arytenoid adduction through the same exposure before closing. Medialization alone corrects the membranous fold but has limited effect on a lateralized or rotated arytenoid.
Close and drain

Irrigate, obtain meticulous hemostasis, and place a small Penrose drain deep to the straps. Loosely approximate the straps in the midline so a hematoma cannot compress the framework, then close platysma and skin. Recheck with the scope for airway caliber, fold position, edema, and mucosal integrity before the patient leaves the room.
Observe the airway

Monitor overnight or for several hours for stridor, neck swelling, or hematoma, since edema around the implant can narrow the glottis in the first day. A perioperative corticosteroid is commonly given to limit edema. Explain that the voice may be strained initially and settles as swelling resolves.
medialization.notes: Replaced with a 15-step sequence from the Iowa Gore-Tex medialization laryngoplasty protocol and its case operative note: awake transnasal-scope monitoring with the face left outside the field, restrained infiltration (fluid itself medializes the fold), window about 5 x 10 mm with lower edge about 3 mm above the inferior border, anterior edge 7-10 mm behind midline, upper edge at fold level; second inferior route through the cricothyroid membrane; strip insertion under the strut; about 2 mm overcorrection; polypropylene hammock fixation; Penrose drain. Disagreement with the current card: the card said to create the window 'without violating the inner perichondrium'; in the Iowa Gore-Tex technique the inner perichondrium is elevated and released posteriorly, inferiorly, and superiorly (not anteriorly), with the mucosa left intact. The step now reflects that. The protocol's perioperative implant soak and intravenous drug doses were left out under the site rule.

steps: Make the template

Trace the normal ear on clear radiographic film and record its position relative to fixed facial landmarks such as the lateral canthus, lateral alar base, and oral commissure. Sterilize the template for use at harvest, carving, and placement. Mark the planned auricular position and axis on the affected side, mirroring the opposite ear.
Prepare the head

Intubate orally with the tube secured in the midline so it does not distort the face. Shave the hairline as needed. Infiltrate dilute epinephrine without lidocaine into the temporal region and around the remnant to reduce bleeding while preserving tissue planes. Plan a skin pocket about 2 cm larger than the framework all around.
Prep and drape both ears

Prep the entire face and both ears into the field so the normal ear can be compared directly for height, projection, and axis throughout the case. Prep the contralateral chest separately for cartilage harvest, and keep the head and chest fields organized so two teams can work if available.
Expose the rib cartilage

Use the contralateral chest so rib curvature suits the helix. Make a 5 to 6 cm incision near the xiphoid along the lower costal margin and divide subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Identify the floating rib for the helical rim and the synchondrosis of ribs 6 to 8 for the base block.
Harvest without pleural injury

Free the cartilage from surrounding muscle and perichondrium with careful blunt and sharp dissection, staying on cartilage and protecting the underlying pleura. Outline and excise the base block using the sterile template. Remove only what the framework needs to limit chest-wall deformity, and keep the floating rib long enough for the full helix.
Test for pneumothorax

Fill the wound with saline and ask anesthesia for a sustained Valsalva breath; bubbling indicates a pleural tear. Repair a tear with a purse-string suture around a red rubber catheter, withdrawing the catheter under suction while the lung is fully inflated, then retest. Close the chest wound in layers; a drain is usually unnecessary.
Carve the base

On the back table, draw the planned ear outline from the template. Carve the base block from the rib 6 to 8 synchondrosis to form the concha, triangular fossa, and scapha, thinning areas to create depth while leaving enough cartilage for rigidity. Keep the framework slightly smaller than the template to allow for skin thickness.
Shape and attach the helix

Trim the floating rib (rib 8 or 9) to a strip about 1 to 1.5 cm wide, curving it with its convex surface inward. Fix it along the base so its lower end reaches the antitragus level and its upper end forms the helical root. Use fine stainless-steel wire and clear nylon, with all knots tied on the deep surface.
Create the skin pocket

Transpose the lobular remnant posteriorly. Raise a thin subcutaneous pocket at the premarked site through a small incision, removing remnant cartilage. Thin the skin enough to show framework detail without buttonholing it, preserve the superficial temporal vessels, and secure hemostasis so a hematoma cannot lift skin off the framework.
Place suction drains

Place two small drains exiting posteriorly through the hair-bearing scalp, plus a larger drain, secured with silk. Suction draws the thin skin envelope into the framework contours and evacuates blood. Pack the pocket with moist gauze until the framework is ready, then confirm drain function before inserting it.
Insert and orient the framework

Slide the framework into the pocket and check it against the template and the opposite ear for vertical height, axis tilt, distance from the lateral canthus, and projection. Adjust before closing, since malposition is difficult to correct later. Confirm the skin drapes over the helix without blanching from tension.
Set the lobule

Bivalve the lobular remnant conservatively to preserve its blood supply, and deliver the lower framework into it. Place a deep stitch beneath the cartilage to seat the lobule upward and backward, two through-and-through stitches fixing it to the posterior skin, and a precise stitch at the lower helix to avoid a notch at the junction.
Close and dress

Advance a small facelift-type skin flap anterior to the ear if needed, close deep tissues with absorbable sutures, and close skin with fine nylon. Confirm all drains hold suction and skin perfusion is good over the framework. Apply a protective mastoid dressing that does not press on the framework.
Monitor and stage

Check the drains, skin color, and pocket for hematoma, skin ischemia, infection, or cartilage exposure, and examine the chest for pneumothorax and pain control. Document the staged plan: elevating the framework with a posterior graft, and tragal and conchal refinement in later stages.
microtia-reconstruction.notes: Replaced with a 14-step first-stage reconstruction from the Iowa microtia protocol: radiographic-film template referenced to facial landmarks, epinephrine-only infiltration, midline oral tube, both ears in the field, pocket about 2 cm larger than the framework, contralateral rib harvest through a 5-6 cm costal-margin incision, saline/Valsalva pleural test with purse-string-over-catheter repair, floating rib helix 1-1.5 cm wide fixed with wire and nylon tied deep, base from ribs 6-8, suction drains through the scalp, lobule transposition and the multi-stitch lobule set. All prior card points kept. Note: Iowa does lobule transposition at stage 1, which differs from strict Brent sequencing (lobule at stage 2); surgeon preference varies. The page is old (last updated before 2017). Later stages are listed but not detailed because the protocol does not describe them.

steps: Assess before surgery

Examine malar projection and width, globe position, vision, extraocular movement, infraorbital sensation, occlusion, and trismus. On CT, review displacement and rotation at the zygomaticofrontal suture, infraorbital rim, zygomaticomaxillary buttress, zygomatic arch, sphenozygomatic suture, and orbital floor. Arrange an ophthalmology examination when the orbit is involved.
Plan the airway

Oral intubation usually works for an isolated ZMC fracture; deviating the mandible away from the injured side can improve mouth opening despite trismus. Be prepared for flexible endoscopic nasal intubation or tracheostomy in combined injuries, poor mouth opening, or when a cervical-spine injury limits positioning. Agree on tube position so it does not block the field.
Choose approaches for each fracture line

Plan to expose every displaced fracture line before plating; a nondisplaced or minimally displaced arch is usually left unexposed. Consent for gingivobuccal, transconjunctival, subciliary, lateral brow or upper eyelid, and hemicoronal options as needed, explaining the lower-eyelid malposition (ectropion) risk of the eyelid approaches.
Open the gingivobuccal sulcus

Incise the upper buccal sulcus with a needle cautery or blade, leaving a 3 to 5 mm cuff of mobile gingiva for a secure closure. Go straight to bone and elevate subperiosteally to expose the zygomaticomaxillary buttress, anterior maxilla, zygomatic body, and piriform rim. Stay out of the buccal fat posteriorly, which herniates and obscures the field.
Protect the infraorbital nerve

As elevation proceeds superiorly, identify the infraorbital nerve at its foramen and dissect around it without traction. Stay out of the nasal cavity at the piriform aperture medially. This exposure gives the buttress for fixation and lets the surgeon see the anterior face of the maxilla to judge reduction.
Expose the rim and orbital floor

Use a transconjunctival incision (with lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis if wider access is needed) to reach the infraorbital rim and orbital floor while protecting the globe with a malleable retractor. Reach the zygomaticofrontal suture through a lateral brow or upper eyelid crease incision, protecting the frontal branch of the facial nerve.
Mobilize and reduce in three dimensions

Disimpact the zygoma with an elevator or bone hook placed beneath the body or arch, or a screw placed in the body. Reduce it in three dimensions, using sphenozygomatic suture alignment along the lateral orbital wall, the arch contour, and the buttress to judge rotation. The rim and zygomaticofrontal suture alone can look reduced while the body remains rotated.
Fix the most reliable point first

Fix the most reliable reference point first, then add plates at the remaining buttresses in sequence, rechecking malar projection against the opposite side after each plate. Use stronger plates at the zygomaticomaxillary buttress and low-profile plates at the infraorbital rim and zygomaticofrontal suture. A hemicoronal approach is reserved for comminuted arches and severe displacement.
Reconstruct the orbital floor

After the zygoma is reduced and fixed, inspect the floor when the fracture pattern, enophthalmos, or entrapment requires it. Free herniated orbital contents and place an implant on stable ledges, including the posterior ledge, without impinging on the orbital apex. Confirm infraorbital rim alignment and restoration of orbital volume.
Check the eye before closing

Perform forced duction testing after floor work and implant placement to confirm free globe movement and no soft-tissue entrapment. Check pupil response and globe position. Any new restriction means the implant or orbital tissue must be adjusted before closure.
Close each approach

Irrigate and obtain hemostasis. Resuspend the midface soft tissue and close the gingivobuccal incision in layers, the transconjunctival incision with canthal repair as needed, and the brow or eyelid incision carefully. Drains are usually unnecessary; two suction drains are placed if a coronal approach was used.
Recover and follow up

Order serial vision checks depending on orbital involvement and manipulation. Prescribe a soft diet for one to two weeks and oral hygiene for the intraoral wound. Treat persistent trismus with jaw-stretching exercises or a jaw-opening device. Obtain postoperative imaging when reduction or implant position is uncertain.
zmc-orif.notes: Replaced with 12 steps. Iowa ZMC protocol supplied: airway planning (oral intubation usually feasible, mandible deviation for exposure, readiness for flexible endoscopic nasal intubation or tracheostomy), the principle of exposing all fracture lines before plating with nondisplaced arch left alone, gingivobuccal incision details (3-5 mm gingival cuff, subperiosteal plane, avoid buccal fat posteriorly, protect V2, avoid entering the nose at the piriform), consent for eyelid approaches with ectropion risk, coronal drains, soft diet, vision checks, and trismus therapy. Limitation: the Iowa page does not describe reduction, fixation order, orbital floor repair, or transconjunctival technique; those steps keep the current card's reviewed content with standard detail added (sphenozygomatic alignment, plate profile, posterior-ledge floor implant, frontal branch protection).

step: Relieve external compression and correct systemic factors

While the OR is being arranged, check for tight tracheostomy tapes, dressings, or ties around the neck. Correct head rotation or flexion that kinks the pedicle, and sit the patient up to about 45 degrees. Treat hypovolemia and hypotension. A tense hematoma threatening the flap or airway may need sutures released right away.
Venous congestion without a revisable cause

If the pedicle cannot be revised, the patient cannot safely return to the OR, or only part of the flap is congested, consider medicinal leech therapy, with ongoing blood loss monitoring and transfusion as needed. Incising the congested flap edge to let it bleed is a temporary bridge, not a substitute for exploration when salvage is feasible.

free-flap-takeback.notes: From the Iowa free flap monitoring and salvage protocol: added correction of systemic factors (hypovolemia, hypotension) to the bedside step, and a new step on leech therapy and temporary flap-edge incision for venous congestion when operative revision is not possible, unlikely to succeed, or only part of the flap is affected. Iowa also lists heparin with or without thrombectomy, thrombolytics, and anastomotic revision, which the card already covers in more detail. Point of difference: Iowa uses routine postoperative aspirin; the card's statement that aspirin has not been shown to improve flap survival was kept because it matches the published evidence and it addresses rescue, not routine postoperative use. Medication cover that usually goes with leech therapy was left out under the site rule; the site owner should decide on it.

step: Other missed-gland sites

Check the space medial to the superior pole (may need upper pole vessel division), the carotid sheath, retropharyngeal space, and the thyrothymic ligament and upper thymus, where transcervical thymectomy retrieves a low inferior gland. Dividing the sternothyroid improves exposure. An intrathyroidal gland may need hemithyroidectomy. Find a marked remnant by its suture; after autotransplant, a high PTH from the grafted arm points to graft recurrence.
Autotransplant devascularized tissue

If a normal gland is devascularized, confirm it is parathyroid, mince it into roughly 1 mm pieces in saline, and implant them into small pockets in the sternocleidomastoid or forearm. Mark the site with a nonabsorbable suture and clips so it can be found on imaging or at any later operation for recurrence.
Interpret intraoperative PTH

Draw post-excision samples about 10 to 15 minutes after removal; PTH half-life is about 5 minutes, and manipulation can spike levels. A fall of at least 50% from the higher of the baseline and pre-excision values, ideally into the normal range, supports cure. If the fall is inadequate, reassess localization and multigland disease before extending into scarred territory.

reop-parathyroid.notes: Iowa parathyroidectomy protocol (no separate reoperative section) added: ectopic sites including the retropharyngeal space and intrathyroidal glands needing hemithyroidectomy, sternothyroid division for exposure, an autotransplant step with suture-and-clip marking to help later localization, and PTH timing (half-life about 5 minutes, manipulation spikes) with the at least 50% or normal-range criterion. Iowa redraws at 15-20 minutes; the step uses 10-15 minutes, the common Miami-criterion timing in US practice, and notes manipulation spikes. Iowa also notes that nerve monitoring is most useful in reoperation, which the card already reflects.

step: Robotic en bloc sequence

For transoral robotic lingual tonsillectomy, incise just behind the circumvallate papillae into the superficial tongue base muscle, then make a midline cut back toward the center of the epiglottis and a lateral release just deep to mucosa at the glossotonsillar sulcus. Dissect from anterior to posterior on a thin layer of muscle so the specimen stays intact.
Release the vallecula last

The vallecular mucosa is the final attachment. Divide it either from anterior while folding the specimen back toward the epiglottis, or by flipping the specimen forward and cutting under direct view into the vallecula. Leave no lymphoid mucosa posteriorly. When searching for an unknown primary cancer, mark the specimen for orientation before it is released.

lingual-tonsillectomy.notes: Iowa TORS lingual tonsillectomy (tongue base mucosectomy) protocol supplied the en bloc incision sequence (circumvallate incision, midline cut toward the epiglottis, lateral release, anterior-to-posterior dissection on a thin muscle layer, vallecular mucosa divided last by either of two routes, orientation marking, next-day discharge for most). Caveat: the Iowa page describes this for an unknown primary carcinoma after a negative workup, not sleep apnea; the inserted steps adapt only the dissection technique, and the orientation marking is flagged for the oncologic use. Used edit mode rather than a full replacement because the card's 14 existing steps are already detailed and recently reviewed.

steps: Choose the reconstruction

Work up the reconstructive ladder first: secondary intention, primary closure, local flap, then graft. Ask about isotretinoin use and note any cautery damage to the bed, because injury to adnexal structures and a heat-damaged bed both impair take. Plan the donor site so the scar is hidden and the patient is comfortable.
Pick full versus split thickness

Template the defect and choose by contour, contraction risk, color and texture match, and bed vascularity. A full-thickness graft matches facial color better and contracts less but needs a well-vascularized bed. A split-thickness graft takes more reliably on a poorer bed but contracts more and may change pigment. Graft survival depends on imbibition, then inosculation, then ingrowth of new vessels.
Prepare the recipient bed

Debride the defect to a clean, well-vascularized base and achieve meticulous hemostasis with the finest bipolar or pressure possible before harvest. Avoid charring the bed with broad cautery. Exposed bare cartilage or bone without perichondrium or periosteum will not support a graft; plan a flap or wait for granulation instead.
Harvest a full-thickness graft

For a facial full-thickness graft, take skin from the preauricular, postauricular, supraclavicular or upper-lid region for color match. Excise an ellipse slightly larger than the template that can be closed primarily, staying in the subdermal plane so little fat comes with the graft.
Defat the full-thickness graft

Drape the graft dermis-up over a finger or a moist sponge and trim all subcutaneous fat with curved scissors until only shiny white dermis remains, without perforating it. Residual fat blocks imbibition and inosculation and is a common reason for partial loss. Keep the graft moist in saline until inset.
Set up the dermatome

For a split-thickness graft, fit the blade guard to the needed width and set depth to about 0.012 to 0.018 inch; about 0.015 to 0.018 inch gives an intermediate graft. Lubricate the blade and the skin with mineral oil, and wipe all prep solution off the donor site so the dermatome glides.
Harvest the split-thickness graft

Choose a large, flat, concealed donor site such as the posterolateral thigh, or the scalp. Run the dermatome at about 30 degrees with gentle, steady downward pressure in one continuous pass. Traction matters: the surgeon tensions skin behind the device while an assistant flattens skin ahead with a tongue depressor, or the assistant tensions the borders with towel clamps.
Finish the harvest

End the pass by angling the dermatome up off the skin, or stop with the blade still engaged and cut the distal edge with a scalpel. Store the graft in saline. Apply gauze soaked in epinephrine or thrombin to the donor site for hemostasis, but not when the donor skin lies on a free flap, where vasoconstrictor could compromise flow.
Orient and trim

Lay the graft dermal side down; the dermis is the shinier, whiter surface. Trim it to fit the defect exactly without folding, stretching, wrinkling, or unnecessary overlap onto normal skin. On the face, avoid meshing for cosmetic reasons; instead pie-crust a split-thickness graft with a few small stab cuts so blood and serum can escape.
Secure the perimeter

Anchor the graft with four corner sutures, then a running or interrupted perimeter suture, for example 4-0 or finer fast-absorbing gut on the face. Place internal quilting or basting sutures so the undersurface stays in complete contact with the bed, especially over concave areas such as the medial canthus or conchal bowl.
Evacuate trapped fluid

Before dressing, roll out any blood or air trapped under the graft with a moist cotton-tipped applicator through the pie-crust cuts or the edges. Obtain hemostasis without lifting the construct repeatedly. Hematoma, seroma and shear are the main causes of graft failure, and all are prevented at this step and the next.
Bolster the graft

Apply a tie-over bolster or contoured pressure dressing that gives uniform, gentle pressure and immobilizes the graft against shear, without ischemic compression of surrounding structures such as the lid, ala or ear. A contoured negative-pressure dressing is an option where it can hold a seal.
Close and dress the donor

Close a full-thickness donor primarily in layers. Dress a split-thickness donor with a moisture-retentive dressing such as a transparent film or foam; occlusive dressings speed healing and reduce pain. Warn the patient about donor pain, fluid weeping, pigment change, hypertrophic scarring and slow healing.
Take down the bolster

Remove the bolster at about 5 to 7 days and inspect for take, hematoma, seroma, infection and shear. A healthy graft is pink and adherent. Dark, blistered epidermis may still survive if the dermis is adherent, so do not debride early. Choose the next dressing by what you see, and protect the graft from sun to limit pigment change.
skin-graft-face.notes: Iowa STSG protocol added dermatome setup (blade guard width, 0.015-0.018 inch intermediate thickness, mineral oil, removing prep solution), 30-degree steady pass with two traction methods, two ways to end the pass, donor hemostasis with epinephrine/thrombin except on free-flap skin, dermal-side identification, corner-then-running fixation, pie-crusting as an alternative to meshing, isotretinoin/cautery risk, graft-survival phases, donor-site complication list. Iowa removes the dressing around day 7; card's 5-7 days kept. Iowa offers meshing; card's 'avoid meshing on the face' kept and pie-crusting used instead. Iowa mentions topical antibiotic ointment after takedown; omitted per site rule. Full-thickness harvest/defatting details retained from the current card (Iowa page is STSG-focused).

steps: Stabilize and prepare

Correct coagulopathy and, with the prescribing team, reverse anticoagulation where safe. Intubate with a cuffed tube to protect the airway from blood. Remove any packing and clear clot with suction under a 0-degree endoscope so the field is clean before injection and the true bleeding site can be judged.
Decongest and inject

Place vasoconstrictor pledgets, then inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine at the middle turbinate insertion and along the uncinate process. A transoral greater palatine canal injection, aspirating first, can further reduce flow from the pterygopalatine fossa. Allow time for vasoconstriction before incising.
Medialize and orient

Medialize the middle turbinate gently. If the corridor is narrow, perform an uncinectomy and maxillary antrostomy so the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus guides you. Palpate the posterior fontanelle region of the lateral wall to find where firm bone begins, just ahead of the sphenopalatine foramen.
Plan the incision

Make the mucosal incision on the lateral nasal wall about 1 cm in front of the posterior end of the middle turbinate, either as a vertical cut from just below the turbinate's horizontal attachment toward the inferior turbinate, or as a U-shaped cut centered on the posterior middle turbinate. Coagulating the mucosa first with bipolar limits bleeding.
Raise the flap

Incise through to bone with a Cottle or suction elevator and elevate a subperiosteal flap posteriorly. Working the flap inferiorly toward the choana first, then sweeping superiorly, keeps the plane clean and delivers the crista ethmoidalis, the small palatine-bone ridge with the foramen directly behind and above it.
Remove the crista

Take down the crista ethmoidalis with a 2-mm Kerrison rongeur and curette to open the anterior margin of the foramen. A small neurosurgical cottonoid placed inferiorly helps retract the flap medially and keeps it out of the instruments. Identify the artery by anatomy rather than chasing active bleeding blindly.
Map every branch

Expose the main trunk and its divisions, including the posterior lateral nasal artery and the posterior septal artery running medially across the face of the sphenoid. Look above and below the main foramen for accessory foramina, which are common and a frequent cause of failure.
Take the anterior branch first
Cauterize and divide the most anterior branch first. It often hides additional branches behind it, which then come into view and can be treated in turn under direct vision rather than missed.
Bipolar along the course

Coagulate each vessel with bipolar along its length and divide it medially, following the branches until you reach the anterior face of the sphenoid sinus. Avoid deep thermal spread into the pterygopalatine fossa. Cautery has been associated with lower rebleeding rates than clips.
If clipping instead

When clips are used, dissect each vessel free around its full circumference before applying the clip, so the clip occludes the whole lumen and does not slip. Partial dissection leads to incomplete occlusion and early rebleeding.
Look for a second source

If the source appears superior or anterior, or bleeding continues, search the septum and ethmoid region and consider anterior ethmoidal artery ligation rather than repeating sphenopalatine cautery. After a pause with blood pressure normalized, reinspect both sides and the nasopharynx.
Replace the flap

Lay the mucosal flap back over the treated vessels and exposed bone, and hold it with a small piece of absorbable packing such as Nasopore or oxidized cellulose. Avoid bulky nonabsorbable packing unless bleeding elsewhere demands it.
Document and plan

Record the branches treated, the method, blood loss and any second source. Document the plan if bleeding recurs: early endoscopy, ligation of the anterior ethmoidal artery, or interventional radiology for embolization of feeding vessels.
spa-ligation.notes: Iowa (page mislabeled 'Anterior Ethmoid Artery Ligation' but describing endoscopic SPA ligation) added: injection sites at middle turbinate insertion and uncinate, palpating the posterior fontanelle, U-shaped incision option with prior bipolar of mucosa, flap elevated toward choana then superiorly, 2-mm Kerrison, inferior cottonoid retraction, treating the anterior branch first to reveal hidden branches, cauterizing to the sphenoid face, 360-degree dissection before clipping, cautery associated with lower rebleeding than clips, flap secured with Nasopore/oxidized cellulose. Epistaxis protocol supports embolization as a fallback. No disagreement with the current card; its vertical-incision option was kept.

steps: Plan before induction

Review prior procedures, autoimmune workup and reflux status; idiopathic stenosis often recurs and needs serial treatment. Agree with anesthesia on the ventilation sequence, typically mask ventilation with full relaxation, then jet ventilation for the endoscopic work, then a small tube for balloon dilation, plus a rescue plan if the lumen is critical.
Expose the airway

Place a Dedo or similar operating laryngoscope with its tip gently separating the posterior vocal folds, giving a straight view into the subglottis for photography and instruments. Protect the teeth and lips, and suspend so the stenosis is centered under the telescope or microscope.
Topical anesthesia

Insufflate about 1 mL of 4% lidocaine onto the larynx and subglottis before instrumentation. This blunts laryngospasm and cough during jet ventilation and the repeated passes that follow, and it lowers the anesthetic depth needed during stimulation.
Document and grade

Before treatment, record the level, length, grade and character of the stenosis: mature, firm scar versus inflamed, friable tissue. Photograph it with a telescope. Note glottic involvement and posterior glottic scar, which change the plan and the risk of damaging the vocal folds.
Measure the stenosis

Use a marked suction catheter against the laryngoscope entrance: mark at the vocal-fold level, again at the upper edge of the stenosis, and again at its lower edge. The first interval gives the distance from the vocal-fold free edge to the stenosis; the second gives stenosis length. This creates a reproducible map for future procedures.
Open a critical lumen first

If the airway is critically narrow, start with gentle rigid dilation using tapered Jackson dilators until a small microlaryngeal tube passes. In a small female larynx, staying at or below about size 36 lowers injury risk; men usually tolerate about 40 to 42, and larger dilators are hard to pass through the laryngoscope.
Inject steroid into the scar

Inject the stenotic segment with triamcinolone diluted to about 10 mg/mL, for example triamcinolone 40 mg/mL mixed one part to three parts with 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine. The epinephrine also limits bleeding from the later incisions.
Biopsy and radial incisions

With microscissors or a laser, make radial cuts through the scar, commonly at 3 and 9 o'clock, adapting the sites to the shape of the narrowing. Paired cuts around a small anterior segment at 12 o'clock allow a biopsy. Divide scar bands radially before dilation, and avoid circumferential mucosal injury that promotes restenosis.
Place a small tube
Intubate with a small microlaryngeal tube, about 4.0 to 5.0, so ventilation continues during balloon work and the glottis is shielded. This reduces glottic injury and avoids a long apneic period.
Position the balloon

Choose a radial-expansion balloon sized to the expected normal lumen, for example 15 to 18 mm in an adult female subglottis. Center it across the stenosis under direct vision so it does not migrate distally or sit on the vocal folds.
Inflate under control

Inflate to the planned diameter and pressure for a controlled interval while maintaining the agreed ventilation or apnea strategy, watching oxygen saturation. Hold, then deflate completely before reassessing; never leave a balloon inflated while saturations fall.
Reassess and repeat only as needed

After deflation, inspect the mucosa, bleeding and the lumen gained. Repeat dilation only if it adds lumen, avoiding progressive mucosal tearing or cartilage injury from oversized dilation. Deep tears expose cartilage and invite worse scarring.
Adjuncts with care

Apply topical mitomycin only when it is part of your protocol, with careful dose and contact control, and keep it off the glottis. Treat reflux when present; esophagoscopy may show esophagitis in these patients.
Finish and plan

Reinspect the entire airway and photograph the result for comparison at the next procedure. Decide on postoperative steroids, observation level and a rescue-airway plan, and schedule follow-up endoscopy, often in clinic, since serial dilations or office steroid injections are typical.

steps: Anesthesia and tube

Use general anesthesia with a small microlaryngeal tube, about 5.0 to 5.5 in women and 5.5 to 6.0 in men, so the tube sits posteriorly and leaves the membranous folds exposed. If a laser will be used, choose a laser-safe tube and agree on low inspired oxygen with anesthesia.
Expose the lesion

Obtain atraumatic suspension laryngoscopy with the largest laryngoscope that fits and the lesion centered. Protect the teeth and lips. Document both folds with a telescope before manipulation, including the contralateral fold, which may hide a reactive lesion.
Define depth under magnification

Under the microscope, palpate and retract to define the lesion's depth and its relationship to the epithelium, superficial lamina propria, vocal ligament and anterior commissure. Cysts sit beneath the epithelium; polyps are usually exophytic and can be removed more superficially.
Polyp: truncate, don't dig

For an exophytic polyp, grasp it gently and cut it bimanually under the microscope at its base, flush with the fold. The goal is a straight free edge without removing extra mucosal cover or lamina propria. Send all tissue for pathology.
Infuse the subepithelial space

For a cyst or deeper lesion, inject saline with dilute epinephrine (about 1:10,000) into the superficial lamina propria. This lifts the epithelium off the lesion, separates the planes, and limits bleeding without distorting the vibratory edge.
Make the cordotomy

Incise the epithelium on the superior surface just lateral to the lesion, at a site that preserves the vibratory edge and leaves the most usable epithelium for redraping. Keep the incision long enough for access but no longer than needed.
Elevate the microflap

Raise the epithelial flap within the superficial lamina propria, separating epithelium from the lesion with fine blunt instruments. Stay out of the vocal ligament. Preserve the overlying epithelium, since it is the cover that will re-epithelialize the fold.
Dissect around the capsule

Separate the cyst capsule bluntly from the underlying superficial lamina propria wherever possible, keeping the capsule intact. Leave a small cuff of soft tissue at the anterior and posterior poles to grasp for traction. Switch to sharp dissection where inflammation has scarred the planes.
If the cyst ruptures

Do not abandon the dissection. Dissect the decompressed capsule carefully off the epithelial basement membrane, removing all lining so the cyst does not recur, while preserving the epithelium itself. Retained capsule is the usual cause of recurrence.
Remove and preserve

Deliver the lesion while preserving normal superficial lamina propria and avoiding extra tissue removal at the medial edge, since lost lamina propria leaves a stiff, scarred vibratory edge that cannot be restored. Send it for pathology.
Minimal hemostasis

Control pinpoint bleeding with epinephrine-soaked cottonoids held gently on the bed, or the least traumatic method available. Avoid broad cautery, which stiffens the fold and harms vibration, and avoid laser near the edge.
Redrape the flap
Lay the microflap back over the bed so the edge lies smooth without tension. Trim only clearly redundant or nonviable epithelium. Reinspect both folds and document the final straight contour.
End suspension and set voice rest

Release suspension before pressure injury to the tongue or teeth. Plan a period of voice rest; Iowa's cyst protocol uses about 2 weeks of complete rest after microflap excision, followed by graded voice use and voice therapy.
Rescue step: airway fire

If an airway fire or sustained flash occurs, announce it and stop laser or energy delivery. Anesthesia stops oxidizer flow and disconnects the circuit; remove the burning tube and debris and flood the airway with saline. Do not continue or pause for imaging during combustion. Then re-establish ventilation, avoiding supplemental oxygen and nitrous oxide when physiology permits.

steps: Position and protect

Position supine with the head fixed in a Mayfield or horseshoe headrest and the bed turned away from anesthesia. Place temporary tarsorrhaphy sutures to protect the corneas. Prep the face and entire scalp, and secure a towel behind the planned incision down to the mastoid regions. Prep the abdomen if fat obliteration is possible.
Design the coronal incision

Mark from helical root to helical root about 2 to 3 cm behind the hairline, using a zigzag or broken-line pattern so the scar hides better when hair is wet. Check the hairline in men; with receding hair, move the line back but warn that the scar may show later. Use an existing laceration only if it gives adequate exposure.
Raise the scalp flap

Incise through galea and raise the flap in the subgaleal plane, leaving pericranium on the skull for a later vascularized flap. Switch to a subperiosteal plane over the sinus and about 2 cm above the supraorbital rims. Close the galea and subcutaneous layer at the end, so preserve a clean galeal edge now.
Protect the frontal branch laterally

Over the temporalis, dissect deep to the temporoparietal fascia and directly on the deep temporal fascia so the frontal branch rides up in the flap. If the arch or lateral orbit is needed, incise the superficial layer of deep temporal fascia just above the arch; entering the fat pad higher bleeds from the middle temporal artery and causes later hollowing.
Release the supraorbital bundles

For exposure of the rims, nasofrontal region and orbital roofs, free the supraorbital neurovascular bundle and reflect it with the flap. If it runs through a bony foramen, take down the inferior bridge with a small osteotome tap. Preserve the supratrochlear bundles too; injury causes scalp and forehead numbness.
Raise the pericranial flap

Elevate a broad, anteriorly based pericranial flap supplied by the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels, as long as the planned coverage requires. Keep it moist and protect its base throughout, since it is the key barrier if the sinus is cranialized or the ducts are plugged.
Define the injury

Expose the anterior table, supraorbital rims and nasofrontal region. Define anterior and posterior table fractures and the outflow anatomy, correlating with the CT. Remove and preserve usable anterior-table fragments in oriented fashion, plating them together if helpful.
Inspect the sinus

Look into the sinus for mucosal injury, posterior-table displacement or comminution, CSF leak and outflow-tract disruption. These findings determine preservation, obliteration or cranialization. Involve neurosurgery when the posterior table is badly comminuted or dura is torn.
Preserve when possible

If the outflow tract is intact or can be restored and the posterior table is stable, preserve the sinus: reduce and fix the anterior table without trapping mucosa behind displaced fragments, and plan endoscopic surveillance of drainage.
Obliterate when outflow is lost

For obliteration, remove every trace of mucosa from all walls and recesses and lightly drill the bone with a burr to clear mucosa in the foramina of Breschet. Invert and plug the frontonasal ducts, then fill the cavity with abdominal fat or another accepted material before replacing the anterior table.
Cranialize a destroyed posterior table

Remove the posterior table back to the anterior cranial fossa floor, strip all mucosa, and drill the inner cortex of remaining walls to clear the foramina of Breschet. Invert outflow mucosa downward, plug both frontonasal ducts with pericranium, muscle or bone, and let the frontal lobe expand into the space after dural repair.
Repair dura and seal the floor

Repair dural tears primarily or with a fascia or pericranial graft for a watertight closure. Turn the vascularized pericranial flap down over the sinus floor and plugged ducts to separate the nose from the anterior cranial fossa permanently. Leave its base free so it is not strangled when the anterior table is replaced.
Restore the contour

Reconstruct the anterior table and supraorbital rims with stable low-profile fixation, bridging small gaps with bone graft or mesh as needed for protection and cosmesis. Check the forehead contour against the opposite side before closing.
Close over drains

Confirm hemostasis and close dead space. Place two perforated suction drains under the coronal flap, close galea and subcutaneous tissue with 2-0 absorbable sutures, and close skin with staples or a running 3-0 nylon. Remove drains when output falls below about 30 mL per 24 hours.
Follow-up and surveillance

Warn the patient about numbness behind the incision, possible alopecia along the scar and frontal-branch weakness. Watch early for hematoma and CSF leak, and document long-term surveillance for mucocele, contour deformity, CSF leak and intracranial infection.
