steps: Expose and inject

Position supine with a shoulder roll and the neck gently extended. Place a Dingman or similar mouth gag, checking the tongue blade does not compress the tongue or endotracheal tube. Infiltrate the planned incisions with local anesthetic containing 1:200,000 epinephrine and wait for vasoconstriction.
Mark the repair

Mark the medial cleft margins, hard-palate relaxing incisions along the alveolar ridge, and the greater palatine neurovascular pedicles before cutting. For the soft palate, choose between straight-line closure with intravelar veloplasty and a double-opposing Z-plasty, which also lengthens the velum and suits narrow soft-palate clefts.
Raise the hard-palate flaps

Elevate oral mucoperiosteal flaps from the relaxing incisions and cleft margins, identifying and preserving the greater palatine pedicles as they exit their foramina. Free them enough for a tension-free midline closure, using gentle pedicle release if more reach is needed.
Close the hard-palate nasal layer

Separate nasal mucosa from the hard-palate shelves and vomer as required, and close the nasal layer with 4-0 absorbable sutures without leaving a gap. The hard and soft palate junction is the most common fistula site, so take extra care there.
Split and freshen the velum

Divide the soft palate along the cleft in the midline back to the uvula, and trim the medial edges and uvular tips to fresh tissue. Identify the abnormal levator veli palatini fibers inserting on the posterior hard palate.
Option A: intravelar veloplasty

Dissect the levator insertions off the posterior hard-palate edge and from the nasal and oral mucosa, then reorient each muscle transversely and suture the two together across the midline as a muscle sling, aligning nasal, muscle and oral layers.
Option B: design the Z-plasties

For a double-opposing Z-plasty, draw lateral limbs at about 45 to 60 degrees from the midline limb, ending behind the alveolar ridge. On one side the oral flap is posteriorly based and carries the muscle; on the other it is anteriorly based mucosa only. The nasal flaps are designed as the mirror image. Steeper angles give more lengthening.
Option B: elevate the oral flaps

On the muscle-carrying side, lift the levator with the oral mucosa off the nasal mucosa, freeing it from the posterior hard-palate edge. On the opposite side, lift only mucosa and submucosa, leaving muscle on the nasal side. A back-cut along the medial alveolar margin can add mobility.
Option B: transpose the nasal layer

Cut the nasal flaps parallel to the bases of their overlying oral flaps. Rotate the nasal myomucosal flap backward and the nasal mucosal flap forward, aiming each tip toward the opposite superior constrictor. This overlaps the two levator bundles and lengthens the velum. Close the nasal layer first, from flap tips toward the midline.
Option B: close the oral layer

Transpose and advance the oral flaps across the midline and close with 4-0 absorbable sutures, placing a stronger buried monofilament stitch near the midline to secure the flaps. Avoid leaving raw nasal surface exposed, which contracts and shortens the palate.
Close the uvula

Freshen the uvular halves and close them with a horizontal mattress suture, aligning nasal, muscle and oral layers without airway-narrowing bulk. A well-aligned uvula is a visible check that the layers have been matched.
Close the hard-palate oral layer

Close the oral mucoperiosteal flaps in the midline from posterior to anterior, securing them without kinking or strangling their pedicles. Lateral relaxing-incision raw areas can be left to heal by secondary intention.
Inspect before release

Check for exposed bone at the closure, pedicle kinking, bleeding and symmetric palatal length and mobility. Avoid tight packing against the repair. Remove the gag and check the tongue for swelling and the teeth and lips for injury.
Postoperative plan

Plan airway observation, since tongue swelling and narrowing of the velopharynx can obstruct breathing, especially in syndromic children. Set hydration, analgesia, arm restraints and a soft feeding plan. Arrange fistula checks and speech follow-up for velopharyngeal function.

steps: Preoperative review

Review CT and MRI for the carotid arteries, optic nerves, cavernous sinus, sphenoid septation and suprasellar extension. Ask about prior nasal trauma, sinus surgery and sinus disease, and identify obstructive sleep apnea and CPAP use, since CPAP must be held after surgery. Confirm the glucocorticoid plan with anesthesia and endocrinology.
Position and set up

Tape the tube to the left lower lip, and place an arterial line (left arm preferred) and Foley catheter when intradural work is expected. Rotate the bed 180 degrees; neurosurgery pins the head in a Mayfield, slightly extended and turned toward the surgeon. Prep the face, and the abdomen or thigh if fat or fascia lata may be needed.
Register navigation

Register the navigation system before prepping, then drape and position the reference array over the field. Recheck probe accuracy at key points, especially after any turbinate resection and intermittently through the case, because anatomy shifts as bone is removed.
Decongest and inject

Place pledgets with oxymetazoline plus either 4% cocaine or 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine. Perform a transoral greater palatine canal injection, aspirating first. Inject the middle turbinate face and axilla and the posterior septum. Use a white-balanced, focused 0-degree endoscope.
Find the sphenoid ostium

Survey both sides for septal deviation and choanal anatomy. Lateralize the middle turbinate with the curved back of a blunt Freer and find the natural sphenoid ostium in the sphenoethmoidal recess, medial to the superior turbinate and about 1.5 cm above the choanal arch.
Manage the turbinates

Gently outfracture the middle and superior turbinates to widen the corridor. Resect the inferior third of the superior turbinate if needed for exposure, and a middle turbinate only when the planned approach requires it. Avoid tearing the superior turbinate high on the skull base, which risks olfactory injury or a leak.
Decide on the flap

If a high-flow leak is likely (extended approach, large suprasellar tumor, planned arachnoid opening), harvest the nasoseptal flap now. Otherwise make a rescue-flap incision that preserves the posterior septal artery pedicle, so a full flap can be raised later if a leak appears.
Harvest the nasoseptal flap

Cut superiorly 1 to 2 cm below the skull base to spare olfactory mucosa, inferiorly along the maxillary crest or nasal floor, and anteriorly as far as size requires. Join the cuts across the rostrum, keeping the pedicle between ostium and choana, elevate subperichondrially, and park the flap in the nasopharynx or maxillary sinus.
Open both sphenoid sinuses

Enlarge each ostium inferiorly and medially, protecting the posterior septal artery below it. Take the rostrum down to the sphenoid floor with a Kerrison or drill and join both sides into one wide opening, extending laterally as the lesion requires.
Posterior septectomy

Remove about 1 to 2 cm of posterior septum with a backbiter, microdebrider or sickle knife on each side so instruments pass through both nostrils. This binarial, two-surgeon technique lets one surgeon drive the endoscope and suction while the other dissects with both hands.
Remove intersinus septa safely

Check the CT for septa that insert on the carotid canal. Bring them flush with the posterior sphenoid wall using a drill or cutting instrument, never by twisting or fracturing, because torque can fracture the canal and tear a dehiscent carotid. Remove sellar-face mucosa only as needed.
Confirm the landmarks

Identify the sella, planum, tuberculum, clival recess, parasellar and paraclival carotid prominences, optic protuberances and lateral opticocarotid recesses. Confirm with navigation, use a micro-Doppler when anatomy is uncertain, and confirm carotid and optic positions with neurosurgery before bone is opened.
Open the sella and assist

Thin the sellar floor with a diamond drill and remove it with Kerrison rongeurs between the carotids. Control intercavernous sinus bleeding before neurosurgery opens the dura. During resection, drive the endoscope, keep the field clear, and watch for CSF, arterial bleeding and the normal gland and stalk.
Grade the CSF leak

Inspect the defect during a Valsalva maneuver and grade it as no leak, low-flow leak through a small diaphragma tear, or high-flow leak from a wide arachnoid or ventricular opening. If an unexpected high-flow leak appears, raise the full flap from the rescue incision.
Reconstruct the skull base

For no or low-flow leaks, use a collagen dural substitute or free fat or fascia graft. For high-flow leaks, build a multilayer repair (inlay and onlay grafts, fat as needed) covered by the nasoseptal flap, laid on bare bone after removing mucosa from the defect margins. Confirm the pedicle is untwisted and not compressed.
Pack and protect

Support the repair with absorbable packing such as Nasopore, plus a balloon or nonabsorbable packing per protocol. Cover the septal donor site with a reverse septal flap or splints. Decide with neurosurgery on a lumbar drain for high-flow defects. Hold CPAP for at least a month to avoid pneumocephalus.

step: Know the high-risk patient

Fistula is more likely after prior radiation, with poor nutrition (albumin below about 3.5 g/dL), anemia (hemoglobin below about 12.5 g/dL), hypothyroidism, diabetes, ongoing smoking, or positive margins. Before the index laryngectomy and again before any repair, correct what you can: nutrition, anemia, thyroid function, glucose and smoking. Plan a salvage case assuming a leak may happen.
Prevent it at the index closure

Close the mucosa with inverting sutures, such as a running Connell-type stitch, in a watertight, tension-free line, saving healthy mucosa. Add a second layer of interrupted absorbable sutures through remaining constrictor and strap muscle. T-shaped and straight closures are both accepted, but the T's three-point junction leaks more, so many prefer a straight closure when feasible.

Iowa's case used a T-type closure successfully; this does not contradict the card's preference for straight closure when feasible. No Iowa page covers fistula repair itself, so steps 2-15 are unchanged.

steps: Stage the injury and plan

Map the deficit, how long the face has been paralyzed, whether a usable proximal facial stump exists, the distal branches, and candidate donor nerves. Within about 30 days favor primary repair; from one month to roughly two years favor bringing new axons to native muscle; beyond about two years plan muscle transfer unless viable distal nerve and muscle are proven by electromyography.
Anesthesia and prep

Ask anesthesia to avoid long-acting paralytics, because a nerve stimulator is used to find and test branches. Position for access to both the face and the donor site, and prep the donor widely: the whole lower leg and foot for sural nerve, the whole arm for medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, so graft length is never limited by the drape.
Find distal branches early

Expose recipient branches in healthy tissue, usually through a preauricular or parotidectomy-type incision with a flap raised over the parotid fascia. In an acute injury, stimulate distal branches before about 72 hours have passed, while they still conduct; tag them with vessel loops and watch which facial region each one moves.
Prepare the proximal stump

Identify the proximal facial nerve and trim back to healthy, pouting fascicles. In oncologic cases send frozen sections of the nerve margins before committing to the graft. Use longitudinal incisions along the nerve course and extend them as needed rather than stair-stepping across the neck or face.
Cut nerve ends cleanly

Under loupes or the microscope, cut each end with a fresh scalpel blade against a firm backstop such as a sterile tongue blade, not with scissors, which crush fascicles. Strip only enough epineurium to align the ends, and match fascicle groups and surface vessels so the two ends sit in their natural rotation.
Decide primary repair or graft

Gaps up to about 1 cm can usually be closed by mobilizing the ends; rerouting the nerve out of the mastoid canal gains about another centimeter but risks devascularizing it. A graft with two suture lines gives better results than a primary repair under tension, so graft any gap that cannot be closed without stretch.
Harvest great auricular nerve

For short single-trunk gaps, the ipsilateral great auricular nerve is the usual donor: similar diameter, two or three fascicles, found crossing the sternocleidomastoid roughly midway between the mastoid tip and the mandibular angle. Its length and branching are limited for multibranch repairs. Warn the patient about earlobe and mastoid numbness.
Harvest sural nerve

For long or branched grafts, take the sural nerve: incise behind and below the lateral malleolus beside the small saphenous vein, loop the nerve, divide it distally, and free it proximally with a tendon stripper or a second calf incision. Up to about 30 cm is available. Use caution in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.
Prepare the graft

Cut the graft to the shortest length that still allows a tension-free repair, store it in balanced salt solution, and reverse its direction so regenerating axons are not lost into side branches. For several distal targets, use a branched segment or split the graft so each cable reaches its own branch.
Perform the coaptation

Place 3 to 4 interrupted 9-0 or 10-0 nylon sutures with about 1 mm bites, using the fewest that hold stable fascicular contact; a perineurial repair suits the proximal trunk and an epineurial repair suits distal branches. If fascicles bulge between the ends, realign or redo the repair. Fibrin sealant may cover the junction, never sit between the ends.
Hypoglossal-facial transfer

When no proximal facial stump exists but distal nerve and muscle are viable, transfer the hypoglossal nerve, ideally at the time of tumor resection. Using part of the hypoglossal nerve or a jump graft spares tongue function and avoids excess drive. Counsel about tongue weakness and atrophy; about 95% regain resting tone and eye protection, with motion beginning at 3 to 6 months.
Masseteric transfer and branch choice

For a masseteric transfer, find the nerve below the zygomatic arch about 3 cm in front of the tragus, deep within the masseter, and divide it distally for length. Coapt to the zygomatic or buccal branches that drive smile and eye closure, and avoid unnecessarily denervating branches that still function.
Cross-face nerve graft

When the proximal nerve is unusable and a spontaneous smile is the goal, stimulate the healthy side's buccal branches and select a redundant one that produces smile without eye or nose movement. Roughly half of those fibers can be sacrificed safely. Tunnel a 15 to 18 cm sural graft through upper-lip incisions and mark its tip with permanent sutures for staged retrieval.
Protect the repair and close

Lay grafts and coaptations in a vascularized, uncompressed bed and check that turning the head or neck does not tension them; with a free flap, coapt after the flap is inset. Place a small drain under the facial flap, close in layers, and apply a light compression dressing. Document the exact donor-recipient construct.
Set expectations and rehabilitate

Facial axons regrow about 1 mm per day: distal repairs may show motion by about 6 months, cerebellopontine-angle repairs up to 18 months, and cross-face grafts 9 to 12 months. Steroids are limited to the perioperative period. Plan facial physical therapy, botulinum toxin for synkinesis, and static support such as an eyelid weight while waiting.

steps: Time the reduction

Reduce either within a few hours of injury, before swelling hides the deformity, or after the swelling settles at about 3 to 10 days (no later than about 14 days in adults; 3 to 7 days in children, whose bones set faster). Pre-injury photographs help; reexamine once edema falls, because early swelling can mask or exaggerate the deformity.
Screen for what closed reduction cannot fix

Exclude septal hematoma, clear rhinorrhea suggesting cerebrospinal fluid leak, naso-orbito-ethmoid and Le Fort fractures, open or severely comminuted septal fractures, caudal septal fracture-dislocation, deviation greater than half the width of the nasal bridge, and presentation beyond two weeks. These need open treatment or delayed septorhinoplasty instead.
Drain a septal hematoma now

A widened, boggy septum with obstruction and ecchymosis is a hematoma until proven otherwise. Incise and evacuate it immediately, then prevent reaccumulation with quilting sutures or bilateral splints, because untreated hematoma leads to cartilage necrosis, abscess and saddle nose.
Choose setting and anesthesia

The reduction can be done in the office, emergency department or operating room under monitored or general anesthesia, with similar functional and cosmetic results. Seat or recline the patient. Examine the external nose and septum, marking sidewall depression, dorsal deviation and points of airway obstruction before anything is manipulated.
Topical decongestion

Lay two narrow pledgets per side along the septum and nasal floor, soaked in oxymetazoline, lidocaine with epinephrine, or 4% cocaine. This shrinks the mucosa so the fracture lines and the septum can be seen and palpated, and it reduces bleeding when the elevator is passed.
Local blocks

Infiltrate 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine at both infraorbital foramina, the supratrochlear nerves and along the nasal dorsum. Wait 10 to 15 minutes for vasoconstriction and full anesthesia. Then palpate inside and out to map which segments are mobile, depressed or overriding.
Measure the elevator

Lay the Boies elevator against the outside of the nose from the alar rim to the depressed nasal bone and mark that depth with your thumb. Its tip must not pass above the level of the medial canthus, which keeps the instrument below the cribriform plate.
Elevate the depressed side

Pass the elevator into the nose on the side of the depressed fragment, lift it outward and forward, and push the opposite, outwardly displaced bone toward midline with the thumb of the other hand. Reduction is often felt as a click. Use controlled force in a stepwise sequence rather than one forceful sweep.
Correct the opposite bone

Reassess after the first side moves. The contralateral nasal bone may need its own outward lift or inward push to center the pyramid and restore dorsal width and projection. Recheck the dorsum by sight and palpation from above and in profile.
Use forceps for impacted fragments

If the elevator will not move an impacted segment, grip the bone with Walsham forceps, one padded blade inside the nose and one outside, and disimpact it with a controlled rocking motion. Avoid crushing the overlying skin and mucosa.
Realign the septum

Assess the septal cartilage; if it is displaced, reduce it at the same time with the elevator or Asch forceps so it does not push the bony pyramid back off midline. Avoid aggressive septal resection in the acute setting. Inspect for mucosal tears, persistent obstruction and nasal valve narrowing.
Internal support if needed

Internal packing or silicone splints are optional and are used for an unstable septum or bleeding. For bleeding, absorbable packing is gentler on the mucosa. Avoid overpacking, which can push fragments back out of position.
Apply the external splint

Paint the dorsum and cheeks with benzoin, lay strips of adhesive tape across the dorsum, then soften a thermoplastic splint in hot water until it turns clear, shake off excess water, and mold it over the tape. Press it gently so it holds the reduction without collapsing the sidewalls.
Aftercare and follow-up

Use ice and head elevation for swelling, and avoid contact sports or glasses resting on the nose while the bones set. Remove the splint and any packing at 5 to 7 days and recheck alignment. Watch for bleeding, perforation, adhesions and saddling. Persistent obstruction or deformity is treated by septorhinoplasty at least 6 months after injury.
closed-nasal-reduction.notes: Iowa added: timing windows (adult and pediatric), contraindication list, office vs operating room equivalence, specific topical and block technique (infraorbital, supratrochlear, dorsum) with 10-15 min wait, Boies depth measured from alar rim, contralateral bone correction, Walsham forceps for impacted fractures, absorbable packing for bleeding, thermoplastic splint sequence, 5-7 day removal, septorhinoplasty at least 6 months later. Iowa's medication advice during packing was deliberately omitted per site policy. Asch forceps and the click/medial-canthus rationale are standard additions. No disagreement with the current card; all current points kept.

step: Peritonsillar collections: limit depth

The pocket usually lies above the tonsil where the anterior pillar meets the base of the uvula; the carotid is about 2 to 2.5 cm posterolateral. Guard the needle so only about 1.5 cm is exposed, aspirate while advancing, never aim laterally or go deeper than 2 cm, then open about 1 cm along the arch, spread to break septations and leave it open.

deep-neck-drain.notes: Iowa has no dedicated deep neck space infection protocol; only the peritonsillar abscess page has drainage technique, so one peritonsillar-specific step was added (target landmark, carotid distance, needle-guard and 2 cm depth limit, incision orientation). Rest of the card left unchanged; no disagreement.

step: CWR: harvest bone pâté first

If you plan canal wall reconstruction with obliteration, collect bone pâté from the mastoid and squamous cortex with a collector before any air cells are opened, so it is free of disease and mucosa. Set it aside. Leave the posterior canal wall thicker than in a routine canal-wall-up case so it survives being cut out and replaced.
CWR: remove the canal wall en bloc

Extend the facial recess down to the canal floor, remove incus and malleus head, and sacrifice the chorda. Elevate canal skin from behind without incising it and lift the annulus to about 6 o'clock. Make interlocking mitered microsaw cuts so the replaced wall cannot fall into the mastoid. The inferior cut threatens the facial nerve; the superior cuts threaten a low tegmen and the geniculate ganglion.
CWR: spacer and fascia first

After all disease is cleared, inspect the removed canal wall segment for adherent matrix. Place a teardrop of thick silicone sheet with its tip in the Eustachian tube orifice; if the stapes superstructure is gone, add a small wedge marking the footplate. Underlay a generous temporalis fascia graft that also covers every bone-cut margin, supported with gelatin sponge.
CWR: block, replace and obliterate

Seal the attic (scutum to tympanic facial nerve) and facial recess with cortical bone chips from the mastoid tip, replace the canal wall, and pack the drained pâté firmly up to the cortex so canal packing cannot push the wall backward. Reposition the canal skin through a long speculum. Contraindications: matrix that cannot be fully removed, prior canal-wall-down surgery, or no second look.

mastoidectomy.notes: Iowa added a canal wall reconstruction (removable posterior canal wall with mastoid/attic obliteration) pathway: pâté harvest before opening cells, thick canal wall, en bloc mitered wall removal and its nerve/dural hazards, silicone spacer and fascia sequence, bone-chip blocking, wall replacement and pâté packing, contraindications. Iowa stages this with a second look at about 6 months (card says 9 to 12 months or diffusion MRI); left the card's staging step alone since both intervals are used in US practice. Iowa's perioperative medication regimen and pâté irrigation solution were omitted per site policy. No lateral semicircular canal fistula or tegmen repair content was found on Iowa pages, so those gaps remain.

steps: Plan from the CT

Before incision, review the CT for skull base height and asymmetry (Keros depth of the olfactory fossa), a dehiscent or medially displaced lamina papyracea, Onodi cells, anterior ethmoid artery position, and the ratio of maxillary to ethmoid height; a low skull base relative to the maxillary roof raises the risk of skull base injury.
Set up and register

With the patient supine, intubated orally and the table turned, register the image-guidance system and confirm accuracy on fixed landmarks. Leave the eyes exposed under clear dressings so they can be checked and palpated during the case. Confirm a plan with anesthesia for controlled blood pressure.
Decongest and inject

After topical decongestion, perform rigid endoscopy on both sides and gently out-fracture the inferior turbinates if access is tight. Inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the lateral nasal wall and the axilla of the middle turbinate. Medialize the middle turbinate gently without fracturing it.
Uncinectomy and maxillary antrostomy

Remove the uncinate process with back-biting forceps or a microdebrider, find the natural maxillary ostium with a curved suction, and enlarge it posteriorly and inferiorly into the natural opening so there is no recirculation. Culture purulence and irrigate the sinus. The antrostomy roof marks the orbital floor height.
Define landmarks

Identify the ethmoid bulla, lamina papyracea, middle turbinate and the orbital floor at the top of the antrostomy. These set the lateral and inferior boundaries and give a starting height well below the skull base before any ethmoid cell is opened.
Open the bulla

Enter the ethmoid bulla in its safe medial and inferior portion and remove its partitions while keeping the lamina papyracea continuously in view laterally. Leave the bulla's roof and the suprabullar region until the skull base has been identified further back.
Anterior ethmoid cells

Clear the anterior ethmoid cells toward the basal lamella, keeping a known superior limit rather than following disease blindly upward. Medially, stay away from the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate, the thinnest bone in the anterior skull base.
Enter the basal lamella

Pass through the basal lamella of the middle turbinate at a controlled inferior and medial point, just above its horizontal portion, when posterior disease requires it. Preserve the horizontal attachment so the middle turbinate remains stable.
Posterior ethmoid and skull base

In the posterior ethmoid, where the skull base is usually higher and easier to see, identify it with image guidance and direct visualization. Recognize that it slopes downward toward the back and may be asymmetric between sides. Watch for an Onodi cell, which can carry the optic nerve.
Clear the roof from back to front

Once the skull base is found posteriorly, take ethmoid partitions off it working posterior to anterior with curettes, through-cutting instruments and a Kerrison punch. Skeletonize rather than strip the skull base mucosa and the lamina, and never pull bone fragments down from the roof.
Respect the anterior ethmoid artery

Near the front of the roof, locate the anterior ethmoid artery. A vessel sitting within the skull base is protected; one hanging in a mesentery below it is at risk of being torn, with retraction into the orbit and orbital hematoma. Handle the area deliberately and avoid powered instruments against it.
Frontal recess

Clear the frontal recess, including suprabullar and agger nasi cell partitions, following the drainage pathway from below with angled endoscopes and instruments. Irrigate and suction the frontal sinus to remove secretions, while preserving mucosa around the drainage pathway to limit scarring.
Sphenoid when indicated

If the sphenoid is diseased, open it through its natural ostium medial and inferior to the superior turbinate attachment, enlarge medially and inferiorly, and inspect it with a 30-degree endoscope before clearing debris. Repeat the full sequence on the other side.
Final inspection and closure

Remove residual partitions while preserving middle turbinate stability and mucosa. Inspect the orbit, skull base and hemostasis, using vasoconstrictor pledgets and suction cautery. Palpate the eyes to confirm they remain soft. Place middle meatal packing or a spacer if needed to keep the turbinate from lateralizing.
endoscopic-sinus-surgery.notes: Iowa added: setup with image guidance, eye checks, injection sites, uncinectomy and natural-ostium antrostomy with culture, posterior-to-anterior clearance off the skull base, frontal recess and sphenoidotomy position, CT risk factors (Keros, lateral lamella, displaced lamina, Onodi cell, anterior ethmoid artery, maxillary:ethmoid ratio), pledgets/suction cautery and middle meatal packing. All current card points kept. Iowa's postoperative medication and mitomycin items were not included.

steps: Review the sphenoid on CT

Before entering, check pneumatization type (a sellar pattern leaves thin bone over the clivus), the side and attachment of intersinus septa, dehiscence of the carotid canal or optic canal, and any Onodi cell. Septa often insert on the carotid prominence, so they must never be twisted or torn out.
Set up

Use image guidance when available and confirm registration. Decongest the nose and inject the region of the middle and superior turbinates with lidocaine and epinephrine. Keep the eyes visible for intermittent checks.
Choose the route

Approach either directly through the sphenoethmoidal recess, medial to the middle and superior turbinates, or through a completed posterior ethmoidectomy. In either case identify the sphenoid rostrum and the face of the sinus rather than drilling into it blindly.
Find the natural ostium

Locate the superior turbinate and the sphenoethmoidal recess. The natural ostium lies medial to the superior turbinate, usually about 1 to 1.5 cm above the choana. Confirm it by direct visualization or a gentle probe directed away from the orbit and skull base.
Enter safely

Enter the ostium with an instrument directed medially and inferiorly. If the ostium cannot be seen, enter low and medially on the face of the sphenoid, close to the septum and just above the choana, where the sinus is reliably present and far from the optic nerve and carotid.
Enlarge medially and inferiorly

Widen the opening medially and inferiorly first with a Kerrison rongeur or mushroom punch. Watch for the posterior septal artery crossing the sphenoid face below the ostium; cauterize it before enlarging further down to avoid troublesome bleeding.
Trim the superior turbinate sparingly

Remove only the inferior portion of the superior turbinate when needed for exposure. Preserve its upper part and the mucosa superiorly, which carries olfactory fibers, and keep the attachment as a landmark for the skull base.
Inspect with angled endoscopes

Look into the sinus with a 30-degree endoscope and identify the carotid and optic prominences, the opticocarotid recess, the sella and the clivus before any lateral or superior instrumentation. Correlate each with image guidance.
Size the opening to the goal

Enlarge the sphenoidotomy to what drainage or skull base access requires, without unnecessary mucosal stripping. For combined ethmoid surgery, the opened sphenoid roof gives a reliable posterior skull base height from which ethmoid dissection can proceed forward.
Clear disease under vision

Remove purulence, inspissated debris and polyps with suction and through-cutting forceps under direct vision, then irrigate gently. Keep powered instruments away from the lateral wall and roof unless the course of the optic nerve and carotid is unequivocally defined.
Handle septa and fungus carefully

Take intersinus septa down only with cutting instruments well away from their lateral insertion, never by twisting. Remove fungal debris by irrigation and gentle suction rather than stripping mucosa from the lateral wall.
Confirm patency and hemostasis

Confirm a widely patent opening and hemostasis, using vasoconstrictor pledgets and suction cautery on the septal artery branches. Check the eyes, and place packing or a spacer only if bleeding or scarring risk warrants it.
sphenoidotomy.notes: Iowa's coverage of sphenoidotomy is limited to its chronic sinusitis operative note and anatomy section: identify the rostrum, open medial and inferior to the superior turbinate attachment and extend medially/inferiorly, explore with a 30-degree telescope, irrigate and remove debris, and the CT risk factors (sellar pneumatization, carotid/optic dehiscence, Onodi cell). The remaining steps restructure the current card (all points kept) with standard US teaching (ostium height above choana, low-medial safe entry, septa inserting on the carotid). Treat this card as partially Iowa-sourced; review if stricter sourcing is required.

steps: Position and protect the airway

Place the patient supine, with the bed turned 90 degrees and the endotracheal tube taped in the midline. A shoulder roll can help extend the neck. In a child with Down syndrome, skip the roll and keep the neck neutral because of atlantoaxial instability. Review any prior cervical films: more than 4 mm of laxity suggests instability.
Suspend the mouth gag

Insert a Crowe-Davis (or McIvor) gag. Choose a tongue blade long enough to lift the tongue base but not so long that it presses on the posterior pharyngeal wall. Check that the teeth, lips, and tongue are not pinched and that the tube stays in the blade's groove. Then suspend the gag and expose both tonsils.
Check the palate for submucous cleft

Look at and palpate the soft and hard palate before you start. A bifid uvula, a translucent midline zona pellucida, or a notch in the posterior hard palate suggests a submucous cleft. Any of these should make you reconsider adenoidectomy or limit it to the upper pad, because full removal can unmask velopharyngeal insufficiency.
Retract the palate and view the nasopharynx

Pass a red rubber catheter through the nose, bring it out of the mouth, and clamp it to retract the soft palate. Put gauze between the clamp and the nasal ala so the ala does not get a pressure injury. With a mirror or endoscope, identify the adenoid pad, choanae, vomer, and both torus tubarius and Eustachian tube openings.
Remove the adenoid

Choose an adenoid curette by sizing it against the maxillary incisor arch. Seat it against the vomer and sweep down with steady pressure, or use a suction cautery, microdebrider, or coblation. Keep off the torus tubarius. Avoid deep or excessive inferior resection in a child at risk for velopharyngeal insufficiency, since that low tissue helps close the palate.
Pack the nasopharynx

Pack the adenoid bed with a tonsil ball or sponge and let it compress the bed while you remove the tonsils. Many surgeons do the adenoid first for this reason, though you can also take the tonsils first. Write down how many sponges you place so every one comes out before emergence.
Optional local infiltration

Some surgeons inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the pillars and behind the tonsil with a curved needle, then wait for vasoconstriction. This can make the plane easier to see and reduce oozing. Aspirate before injecting, and keep the needle shallow because the great vessels lie lateral to the tonsillar bed.
Grasp and incise the superior pole

Grasp the upper pole with a curved Allis clamp and pull it medially and down to tent the anterior pillar mucosa. Open that mucosa over the tonsil capsule with a sickle knife, a #12 or #14 blade, or a monopolar needle. Keep the cut close to the tonsil so you save pillar muscle and avoid scarring that can distort the palate.
Find the capsular plane

Spread into the loose areolar layer between the white tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor fascia with a hemostat, Fischer knife, or scissors. The right plane separates almost bloodless with gentle spreading. If you see muscle fibers on the specimen side, you are too deep: move back onto the capsule before going on.
Dissect superior to inferior

Keep pulling the tonsil medially while you work along the capsule from the upper pole toward the lower pole, using cold steel, monopolar or bipolar cautery, or coblation. As each vessel crossing into the capsule comes into view, coagulate it with guarded bipolar or seal it with the energy device before cutting. With monopolar, leave the fibrous layer of the bed intact.
Intracapsular alternative

For obstructive sleep-disordered breathing, some surgeons use an intracapsular (partial) technique. They remove tonsil tissue with a microdebrider or coblation and leave a thin rim of tissue on the capsule. This protects the constrictor and reduces pain and late bleeding. Remove enough to open the oropharyngeal airway, and tell the family that the tonsil can grow back.
Divide the inferior pole

The lower pole merges with lingual tonsil tissue and has a constant arterial supply. Close a Tydings snare across it, or coagulate it with bipolar and then cut it with scissors. Do not dig into the tongue base. Put a tonsil ball in the fossa for pressure, then remove the other tonsil the same way, keeping the capsular plane on both sides.
Secure tonsillar fossa hemostasis

Take out the sponges one at a time. Pull the pillars apart to see the whole fossa, including the lower pole, then coagulate each bleeding point with suction cautery. Avoid broad, deep cautery, which increases pain and the risk of late bleeding. A figure-of-eight 3-0 chromic stitch is only rarely needed. Some surgeons inject bupivacaine into the pillars for pain relief.
Adenoid bed hemostasis and choanal check

Remove the nasopharyngeal pack and look at the adenoid bed again with the mirror or endoscope. Cauterize only the points that are bleeding. Confirm that the choanae are open and no residual tissue blocks them, and that there is no loose tag that could be aspirated. Then irrigate the nasopharynx and look for clots that hide a bleeding site.
Relax suspension and recheck

Release the gag briefly, or have anesthesia give a Valsalva breath, so the vessels refill at closer to normal pressure. Then suspend again and look at both tonsillar fossae and the nasopharynx. Bleeding that the retractor had tamponaded will show now, while it is still easy to control.
Finish and hand off

Irrigate and suction the oropharynx and nasopharynx, suction the stomach to remove swallowed blood, and take out the catheter and gag. Count the sponges. Check the teeth, lips, gums, and tongue for injury, wipe the mouth, apply ointment to the lips, and confirm there is no active bleeding before extubation.
tonsillectomy-adenoidectomy.notes: Built from the Iowa Tonsillectomy and Adenoidectomy protocol: its shared setup and its six surgeon dictation templates (cold steel, Fischer knife, monopolar, bipolar, coblation). Iowa added the 90-degree bed turn, the shoulder roll and the Down syndrome neck precautions (over 4 mm atlantoaxial laxity), sizing the gag blade so it does not touch the posterior pharyngeal wall, red rubber catheter palate retraction with gauze to protect the ala, sizing the adenoid curette against the maxillary incisors, packing the nasopharynx while the tonsils come out, optional lidocaine-epinephrine infiltration, opening the superior pole with a sickle knife or blade, removing the inferior pole with a Tydings snare, rare chromic suture ligation, optional bupivacaine in the pillars, and suctioning the stomach before emergence. Iowa usually does the adenoid first. The card did the tonsils first; both orders are acceptable, and the steps now take the adenoid first. All prior card points are kept: submucous cleft check, capsular plane, intracapsular option, torus and velopharyngeal insufficiency precautions, targeted cautery, release-and-recheck, and the dental check. Iowa's tannic acid step was left out as an institutional preference. No disagreement with the card.

steps: Confirm the diagnosis and airway

Peritonsillar abscess usually presents with trismus from medial pterygoid spasm, muffled voice, bulging of the soft palate on one side, and the uvula pushed to the other side. Before you drain at the bedside, make sure the patient is breathing comfortably and can cooperate. Take a patient with stridor, a child who cannot cooperate, or severe trismus to the operating room.
Image selectively

Ultrasound, done through the mouth or through the neck, helps separate abscess from cellulitis. An abscess appears as a fluid space with no echoes and an irregular border, and ultrasound before aspiration improves the success rate. Get a contrast CT if neck pain is marked on turning, swelling is bilateral, the findings are unusual, or parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spread is suspected.
Set up before you start

Gather a headlamp, a Yankauer suction already running, topical spray and viscous lidocaine, 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine on a 27-gauge needle, and a 10 mL control syringe with an 18-gauge needle. You also need a #11 or #15 blade and a curved hemostat. The patient can sit upright, which lets them spit, or lie down, depending on what you prefer.
Know the target and the danger

The abscess usually sits above and in front of the tonsil, deep to the mucosa and palatoglossus muscle. The typical spot is where a horizontal line from the base of the uvula meets the anterior pillar. The internal carotid lies about 2 to 2.5 cm posterolateral to this spot, so every needle and blade stays shallow and does not angle laterally.
Topical anesthesia and sedation

Spray the area with topical anesthetic or have the patient gargle viscous lidocaine. Then press the tongue down with a blade to see the bulge. If you give IV opioid or benzodiazepine for anxiety and pain, monitor the patient, and give small doses so the patient can still guard the airway.
Infiltrate local anesthetic

Inject lidocaine with epinephrine into the mucosa over the most swollen point, then a little into the muscle beneath it. Hold the suction at the injection site the whole time, because pus may well up during the injection and could be aspirated. If pus appears, aim your aspiration needle at that spot.
Limit needle depth

Trim the needle cap or bend the needle so only about 1 to 1.5 cm of needle can go in. That keeps the tip well short of the carotid. Never go deeper than 2 cm, and point the needle straight back or slightly medially, never laterally toward the parapharyngeal space.
Aspirate the superior pole first

Put the 18-gauge needle in at the point of greatest bulge, usually above the tonsil, and advance about 1 cm while pulling back on the plunger all the time. Drain as much pus as you can. Confirm that you have pus before you make the opening bigger, since a dry tap may mean the swelling is cellulitis.
Manage a dry tap

If the first pass is dry, try a second spot a little lower, at the middle pole, and change the angle slightly. Do not go deeper or more lateral. If two or three passes are dry, stop and get ultrasound or CT before probing further. Many dry taps are cellulitis that will respond to antibiotics and steroids.
Incise at the confirmed site

Take out the needle and make an incision about 1 cm long, parallel to the palatal arch, at the spot where you found pus. Tape the #11 blade so only its tip is exposed, which limits depth. Cut through the mucosa only, not deep and lateral.
Spread and break loculations

Put a curved hemostat into the cavity, open the jaws to widen the tract, and break up any loculations. Press gently around the incision with the Yankauer tip to squeeze out more pus and suction it as you go. Leave the incision open to keep draining; do not suture or pack it.
Culture and irrigate

Send pus for culture if it will change management, for example in recurrent abscess, failed prior treatment, an immunocompromised patient, or an unusual presentation. Group A streptococcus is the most common single organism, but mixed oral aerobes and anaerobes are typical. Irrigate the cavity only when it is large or the pus is thick.
Reassess before discharge

Check that the airway is clear, oozing has stopped, trismus has improved, and the patient can swallow liquids. A patient who can drink, breathe comfortably, has no signs of sepsis, and is not bleeding can usually go home. Start therapeutic antibiotics that cover streptococci and oral anaerobes, and arrange early follow-up.
Escalate when drainage fails

Perform a quinsy (abscess) tonsillectomy under general anesthesia if drainage fails or the abscess comes back. Also consider it for repeated peritonsillar abscess, for prior recurrent tonsillitis, or when an uncooperative child cannot be drained awake. Get a CT and an urgent neck evaluation for neck swelling or worsening pain, which suggests parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, or mediastinal spread, jugular vein thrombophlebitis, or necrotizing infection.
pta-drainage.notes: Built from the Iowa Peritonsillar Abscess (Tonsil Abscess) protocol. Iowa added: the target landmark (where the uvular base meets the anterior pillar, deep to palatoglossus) and the carotid at about 2 to 2.5 cm posterolateral; ultrasound to tell abscess from cellulitis, with better outcomes when it is used before aspiration; CT criteria; the equipment list; suction held ready during injection because pus can drain and be aspirated; continuous negative pressure while advancing about 1 cm; an absolute limit of 2 cm with no lateral angle; a roughly 1 cm incision along the arch; hemostat spreading, Yankauer pressure, and leaving the incision open; Streptococcus pyogenes as the most common single organism; and discharge criteria. Small difference: the card limited the exposed needle to about 1 cm, while Iowa trims the cap to leave 1.5 cm exposed and advances about 1 cm. The step now says 1 to 1.5 cm exposed and never more than 2 cm. Iowa does not describe the quinsy tonsillectomy technique, so the escalation step lists only indications. Taping the blade and the dry-tap, middle-pole sequence come from the prior card and standard US practice, not from Iowa.

steps: Preoperative safety check

Ask about bleeding history, prior anesthetic problems and a recent upper respiratory infection, which raises the risk of laryngospasm. In children with Down syndrome, review neck imaging: more than 4 mm of atlantodental laxity suggests atlantoaxial instability, but because flexion-extension films are insensitive, apply neck precautions to every child with Down syndrome regardless of the films.
Airway and positioning

Secure an oral endotracheal tube exactly in the midline and bring it down over the chin so the tubing leaves the field. Turn the table 90 degrees. A shoulder roll improves extension and the view; omit it and keep head tilt minimal in Down syndrome or any suspected cervical instability.
Place the mouth gag

Insert a Crowe-Davis gag with a blade long enough to control the tongue base but not so long that it presses on the posterior pharyngeal wall. Suspend it, adjust the tongue with a Hurd retractor if needed, and confirm with anesthesia that the tube is not kinked or displaced.
Assess the palate

Palpate the hard and soft palate for a midline notch and inspect for a bifid uvula or a translucent midline zone. These signs of submucous cleft are a relative contraindication: consider a limited superior adenoidectomy that spares the inferior pad, or not removing adenoid at all, because velopharyngeal insufficiency may follow.
Retract the soft palate

Pass a red rubber catheter through the nose, retrieve it from the mouth and clamp it to lift the soft palate atraumatically. Put a gauze between the clamp and the nostril so the alar rim is not pressure-injured, and avoid excessive tension on the velum.
Survey the nasopharynx

Use a laryngeal mirror or an endoscope to see the adenoid pad, both choanae, the posterior vomer and both torus tubarius with their Eustachian tube orifices before removing anything. Judge the size of the pad and how much it obstructs the choanae, which defines how much tissue must come out.
Remove the central pad

Size the adenoid curette to the space, using the maxillary incisor width as a guide. Seat it high in the vault against the posterior vomer and sweep down along the posterior wall in one controlled pass, removing the central obstructing tissue from superior to inferior. Microdebrider or suction cautery ablation under mirror or endoscopic view are alternatives.
Protect the Eustachian tubes

Preserve tissue around the torus tubarius and do not curette or cauterize deeply in the lateral recesses. Deep lateral injury can scar the Eustachian tube orifice and cause tubal stenosis. Stay superficial to the prevertebral fascia so the cervical spine and its ligaments are not exposed.
Respect the inferior limit

Avoid an aggressive inferior resection when velopharyngeal competence is at risk, as with submucous cleft, hypotonia or neuromuscular disease. Leaving a band of inferior adenoid preserves the cushion the velum closes against, and reduces the chance of hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation after surgery.
Pack the bed

Place a tonsil ball firmly in the nasopharynx for pressure hemostasis while waiting, or while the tonsillectomy is done in a combined case. Count the packs so none is left behind in the nasopharynx at the end of the case.
Inspect and control bleeding

Remove the pack and re-inspect with the mirror or endoscope for residual choanal tissue and tags, which can be removed with a smaller curette or forceps. Use targeted suction cautery on bleeding points, keeping power modest and staying away from the torus.
Irrigate and confirm packs out

Irrigate the nose and nasopharynx and suction clots from the nasopharynx and oral cavity. Confirm every pack has been removed and no active bleeding remains, then pass a suction catheter into the stomach to empty swallowed blood, which reduces postoperative nausea and vomiting.
Release and final check

Release the suspension and remove the catheter, then recheck the oropharynx and nasopharynx after a moment, because bleeding can reappear once pressure on the tongue and palate is relieved. Check the lips, teeth, gums and tongue for injury, clean the mouth and return the patient to anesthesia.
adenoidectomy.notes: Iowa (embedded in its tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy protocol and dictation) added: recent upper respiratory infection and laryngospasm risk; Down syndrome neck precautions (no shoulder roll, minimal tilt, more than 4 mm laxity suggests instability, precautions for all because flexion-extension films are insensitive); midline tube and 90-degree table turn; Crowe-Davis blade sizing and Hurd retractor; gauze to protect the ala from the catheter clamp; curette sizing by the maxillary incisors; tonsil-ball pack then suction cautery; irrigation, stomach suction and final oral injury check. Iowa does not describe limits at the torus or the inferior pad, mirror or endoscope technique, or the microdebrider; those points come from the existing card and were kept. No disagreement with the current card.

steps: Review the CT

Before scrubbing, check the uncinate attachment, infraorbital ethmoid (Haller) cells, accessory ostia, a dehiscent or medially displaced lamina papyracea, the Keros depth and skull-base asymmetry. A displaced lamina can look like an ethmoid septation and lead to orbital entry. Plan image guidance for revision surgery, distorted anatomy or extensive polyposis.
Set up the room

Intubate orally, position supine and turn the table 180 degrees. Leave both eyes uncovered (taped shut, not draped) so the globes can be seen and palpated during dissection. Register the navigation system if it is used, and confirm accuracy on fixed landmarks before cutting.
Decongest and inject

Place oxymetazoline-soaked cottonoid pledgets along the middle meatus. Then inject 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the lateral nasal wall at the uncinate and into the axilla of the middle turbinate on each side, and wait several minutes for vasoconstriction before starting.
Diagnostic endoscopy

Make a first pass along the nasal floor to see the nasopharynx and Eustachian tube openings, then a second pass to view the middle turbinate, osteomeatal complex, superior meatus and sphenoethmoidal recess. Identify the middle turbinate, uncinate process, ethmoid bulla and the expected region of the natural maxillary ostium before cutting.
Create working room

Medialize the middle turbinate gently with a Freer elevator without fracturing its skull-base attachment, because the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate is the thinnest bone in the anterior skull base. Lateralize the inferior turbinate if access is tight. Avoid raw mucosa on the turbinate that could scar to the lateral wall.
Remove the uncinate

Palpate the free edge with a ball probe and remove the uncinate in a controlled fashion with a back-biting forceps or by incising and swinging it medially. Keep the anterior cut behind the hard bone of the nasolacrimal duct, and keep instruments parallel to the lamina so nothing is pushed laterally into the orbit.
Clear the remnants

Trim the horizontal and superior uncinate remnants with through-cutting forceps or a microdebrider with the blade facing medially, away from the lamina. A retained horizontal remnant is the usual reason the natural ostium cannot be found, and it is a common cause of a missed ostium at revision surgery.
Find the natural ostium

With a 30- or 45-degree scope, find the natural ostium with a curved suction or ball probe in the posterior infundibulum, roughly level with the lower edge of the middle turbinate. Do not create a separate accessory opening and assume it is the ostium, since a posterior fontanelle opening is easily mistaken for it.
Enlarge the ostium

Widen the natural ostium posteriorly and inferiorly with straight through-cutting forceps, a back-biter and the microdebrider, sizing the opening to the disease. Join any accessory ostium to the natural ostium so mucus is not carried out one opening and back in through the other (recirculation).
Respect the boundaries

Keep the anterior limit behind the nasolacrimal duct; stop when the back-biter meets hard bone. Keep the superior dissection oriented to the orbital floor and lamina, and avoid extending far posteriorly toward the posterior lateral nasal branches of the sphenopalatine artery, which cause brisk bleeding.
Inspect and clear the sinus

Use angled scopes to look inside the sinus. Evacuate thick pus with a suction trap and send it for culture, then irrigate copiously. Remove only disease that needs direct treatment, such as polyps or fungal debris, and do not strip healthy sinus mucosa, which leads to scarring and poor mucociliary clearance.
Confirm patency and the orbit

Confirm the antrostomy is circumferentially patent and clearly includes the natural ostium. Palpate the globes intermittently through the case and at the end; they should stay soft without proptosis or periorbital bruising. Pressing on the globe while watching the lamina for movement or fat helps detect a dehiscence.
Hemostasis and spacer

Control bleeding with oxymetazoline pledgets and suction cautery while preserving middle meatal landmarks. A dissolvable spacer in the middle meatus can control ooze and keep the middle turbinate medial, limiting opposing raw surfaces. Recheck before extubation and remove all pledgets as the patient is awakened.

Iowa gives no uncinectomy direction or enlargement limits; those, and the nasolacrimal and recirculation points, come from the current card. No disagreement.

steps: Confirm readiness and airway plan

Before incision confirm the child has tolerated decannulation for months, including through sleep and respiratory illness, and review the endoscopy findings. If suprastomal collapse, granulation or subglottic stenosis was found, treat it first or reconsider closure. Agree with anesthesia on oral intubation with the cuff below the fistula, or a mask or laryngeal mask airway for small tracts.
Position and infiltrate

Place a shoulder roll to extend the neck and bring the trachea forward, prep from chin to sternal notch, and keep the anesthesia circuit accessible. Probe the tract gently to judge its length and direction. Infiltrate the skin around the stoma with lidocaine and 1:100,000 epinephrine to reduce bleeding in the superficial layers.
Topical tracheal anesthesia for awake cases

When an older child or adult is closed under local anesthesia, sit the patient semi-upright and spray 4% lidocaine into the trachea through the fistula before infiltrating the skin. This blunts the cough reflex, so the patient is less likely to cough or strain against the repair during dissection and suturing.
Mark and incise an ellipse

Mark an elliptical incision around the fistula with its long axis in a horizontal skin crease, taking only a narrow margin of normal skin. Short horizontal extensions on each side make skin closure easier and leave a flatter scar. Incise through the dermis around the full circumference.
Dissect the tract

Grasp the skin island and use it as a handle. Dissect around the tract through subcutaneous fat with fine scissors or needle cautery, keeping close to the tract wall. In children the tract is usually short; follow it straight down between the separated strap muscles to the anterior tracheal wall.
Protect nearby structures

With a low or wide stoma, the thyroid isthmus and anterior jugular veins can lie against the tract; ligate or cauterize them rather than tearing them. With a high stoma, identify the cricoid above so you do not dissect into the cricothyroid region. Keep the dissection midline, away from the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Excise at the tracheal wall

Divide the tract flush with the tracheal wall and send it for pathology. Confirm no skin lining remains at the opening, because retained epithelium prevents healing and causes recurrence. Trim granulation at the tracheal edge, but avoid enlarging the opening or cutting into neighboring tracheal rings.
Choose the closure method

Primary layered closure suits most small to moderate tracts and heals with a neater scar. Healing by secondary intention avoids trapping air under a sealed skin closure and usually shortens the hospital stay, at the cost of a wound that takes weeks to close. Pooled outcomes for closure rate and complications are similar, so surgeon preference and airway stability guide the choice.
Close the tracheal opening

For primary closure, close the tracheal opening or the soft tissue directly over it with interrupted absorbable sutures, inverting any remaining mucosa toward the lumen. Do not narrow the trachea; with a large defect, closing perichondrium and pretracheal tissue or rotating a local muscle flap avoids pulling cartilage edges together and distorting the airway.
Leak test

Fill the wound with saline and ask anesthesia to give a sustained positive-pressure breath. Bubbling means the closure leaks; add sutures or a muscle layer until it is airtight. A trachea that still leaks under a sealed skin closure is the main cause of subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum.
Strap muscles and air escape

Bring the sternohyoid muscles together in the midline over the tracheal repair as a second layer. Some surgeons place a small passive drain or leave a short gap in the skin closure so any leaked air can escape through the wound rather than tracking into the neck and mediastinum.
Close the skin

Close the subcutaneous layer and skin with absorbable sutures without tension, everting the edges to limit a depressed scar. Apply a light dressing that can be lifted to inspect the neck; avoid a bulky compressive dressing that would hide early swelling or crepitus.
Secondary-intention variant

If healing by secondary intention, after excising the epithelium leave the tracheal opening and skin open or loosely approximated and cover with a light nonocclusive dressing. Expect air bubbling and drainage through the wound for days to weeks; most close within a few weeks, sometimes leaving a wider, depressed scar that can be revised later.
Skin-level closure variant

For a small mature tract under local anesthesia, freshen the scar and make an ellipse that starts at the skin-mucosa junction on the lateral edge and curves medially, with both ends in normal skin. Undermine lightly, use bipolar cautery, then close in one layer with a few vertical mattress sutures that catch deep tissue to close dead space.
Leave a planned air leak

In the skin-level variant, deliberately approximate the skin loosely rather than airtight, so that air escaping from the trachea vents through the wound instead of tracking into the neck. Nonabsorbable 4-0 sutures are usually enough in two or three bites and are removed in 7 to 10 days.
Smooth emergence and handoff

Ask anesthesia for a smooth extubation that limits coughing, bucking and positive pressure. Examine the neck for swelling and crepitus before leaving the room. Hand off the plan: continuous pulse oximetry overnight, a chest x-ray for any crepitus, and opening the skin closure promptly if subcutaneous emphysema develops. After a local-anesthesia closure, observe about an hour for subcutaneous emphysema before discharge.

step: Expose the nerve without making false nerves

Pull the paratracheal tissue laterally toward the carotid and the trachea medially to open the tracheoesophageal groove. Spread the hemostat across the expected course of the nerve, not along it, because repeated spreading in line with the nerve creates fibrous strands that mimic it. Confirm by stimulation, with a laryngeal twitch felt behind the cricoid or an electromyography response.
Nerve anatomy reminders

The left nerve runs more medially, parallel within the tracheoesophageal groove; the right runs obliquely from lateral. A nonrecurrent nerve occurs almost only on the right and always with a retroesophageal subclavian artery, so check prior imaging. The nerve may lie in front of, behind or between inferior thyroid artery branches and may branch before entry; preserve every branch.
Berry ligament

The nerve passes deep to the ligament in most patients, through it in about a quarter, and briefly inside the capsule in some. Use minimal traction on the lobe and divide the ligament sharply or with careful bipolar while following the nerve into the larynx, behind the cricothyroid joint. Old isthmus stump or tissue on the trachea is scarred here.
When the nerve is tethered to the gland

If the nerve is pulled medially into a knuckle against the ligament, release traction and shave the thyroid off the ligament with a knife, staying on the gland side of the nerve, then use bipolar for hemostasis. A remnant of tissue this small is acceptable; it usually shows only about 1% uptake and is ablated by radioactive iodine.
Remove all remaining thyroid

Take the pyramidal lobe (present in about half of patients, often missed at the first operation), any isthmus remnant and tissue at the old resection margin. Residual thyroid beyond a tiny ligament remnant undermines radioactive iodine ablation and thyroglobulin surveillance. Inspect the specimen for parathyroid tissue before it leaves the field.
